+ Gothic-fantasy-humour: Court of the Dreaming — Score: 82.8
Prompt:
Court of the Dreaming: Territorial Dream Dispute. Write a dark fantasy scene with comedic elements set in the Courts of Dream where a case is being heard to determine ownership of a contested dreamscape. Mora, the Slavic nightmare spirit who sits on sleepers' chests causing paralysis and terror, has recently invaded and subverted a carefully crafted recurring dream of a schoolboy, Max. The dream originally featured the boy lying in a field of wildflowers with his crush, always culminating in a muddled almost-kiss and a pleasant confusion of emotions. This dream was the meticulous work of "First Love" (a rosy-cheeked, slightly bashful entity who crafts formative romantic experiences). However, Mora has recently infiltrated the dreamscape, transforming the scene so that when the girl playfully mounts the boy, she morphs into a terrifying yet somehow still confusingly attractive vision who proceeds to sit on his chest and feed on his breath. Mora's defense largely consists of the practical argument that "a girl's gotta eat too, you know?" Write this scene as it unfolds in the courtroom of the Dreaming, with Dream's demeanour, typically impenetrable, betraying a sense of irritation at having to adjudicate such matters. The comedy should derive from the farcical situation, familiar elements of courtroom drama intersecting with the fantastical world of the Dreaming, and the droll portrayal of the characters and their interactions. The humor should be dark and understated throughout. Dream is tempted to some mischief in the resolution of the case. Use descriptives sparingly when setting scene. Write for readability & engagement. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The Court of the Dreaming is called to order at the hour when mortals call it three in the morning and dogs call it nothing at all. Dream sits on a bench carved from a recurring lullaby. His face has the patience of a closed eye. Around him, the vaulted ceilings listen. First Love stands at the plaintiff’s table, cheeks pink, fingers tangled in a ribbon of dawn. Before him lies a model of the dreamscape: a meadow, a schoolboy, a girl, the exact angle of an almost-kiss. Mora sits at the defense table, or rather perches, knees drawn up, chin on them, like a bird considering a worm. Mora emits faint cackles that echo uncomfortably through the vaulted ceilings. The clerk, a thin creature of eyelashes, reads the charge: “Territorial dispute, Dream Registry 771-M: Max, Meadow, Romantic Confusion, Variant: Pleasant. The plaintiff alleges unlawful entry, mood alteration, and consumption of breath.” “My lord,” First Love says, “I built that dream from first principles. The wildflowers took a fortnight. Each petal is a hesitation. The girl’s laugh is tuned to his secret hope. The culmination is not a kiss but the almost, which is the entire point.” Dream says, “Proceed.” “Then this—” First Love points at Mora “—arrived, sat upon the boy’s chest, and turned the beloved into a suffocating omen.” Mora says, “A girl’s gotta eat too, you know?” Cackles. Dream says, “The Court notes the defendant’s argument is not, strictly, a legal argument.” Mora says, “It’s metabolic.” Dream says, “It is also irritating.” Exhibit A is unrolled: a strip of dream-memory. The meadow blooms in miniature. Max lies among flowers, face soft with the terror of being near another person. The girl leans over him, laughing. Then her outline darkens. Her hair becomes moths. Her smile gains too many implications. She settles on his chest. His breath thins. His heart performs the arithmetic of adolescence: fear plus longing divided by no adult supervision. First Love says, “Objection. She is feeding.” Mora says, “I am participating.” Dream says, “On his sternum.” Mora says, “Excellent acoustics there.” Dream’s finger taps once. The exhibit freezes. “Defendant, did you receive permission to enter the dream?” Mora says, “I received an invitation.” First Love says, “From whom?” Mora says, “The boy. He stayed up too late, skipped supper, and thought about her until his nerves tasted like burnt sugar. That’s an invitation. In my jurisdiction.” First Love says, “Your jurisdiction is paralysis and dread.” Mora says, “And yours is awkward hand placement. We are neighbors.” First Love blushes. Dream’s demeanour remains typically impenetrable, but a small star above his shoulder dims—a sign those who knew him would have recognized as irritation. Or indigestion. In Dream, they are often the same. Dream says, “The plaintiff claims ownership by craft. The defendant claims ownership by… appetite.” Mora says, “Sweat equity.” Dream says, “There is no sweat in the record.” Mora says, “There will be.” First Love says, “My lord, this dream is formative. It is meant to teach Max that tenderness can be bewildering, not that tenderness will crush him while wearing his crush’s face.” Mora says, “It still teaches bewildering. More efficiently.” Dream says, “You transformed the romantic lead into a predator.” Mora says, “I gave her depth.” First Love says, “You gave her ribcage.” Mora says, “He noticed it. That’s more than he noticed the flowers.” Dream closes his eyes. The courtroom holds its breath. Somewhere far off, a sleeping child turns over. Dream says, “Counsel, approach the bench.” They approach. First Love smells of warm paper and embarrassment. Mora smells of cold linen and the space under beds. Dream lowers his voice, which somehow makes it more oppressive. “I have judged wars of sleep, stolen lullabies, wardrobe property rights. I did not create this office to arbitrate whether a schoolboy’s yearning belongs to a cherub or a hag.” Mora says, “Cherub and hag are both seasonal labor.” Dream says, “Silence.” First Love says, “My lord, if she is permitted to subvert a formative romantic dream, the precedent will be catastrophic. Next, first kisses will taste of grave soil. Weddings will be haunted by unpaid breath debts.” Mora says, “They already are.” Dream looks at the frozen dream. Max’s face is caught between ecstasy and asphyxiation. The girl-Mora thing hovers above him, uncertain whether to kiss him or collect him. Dream feels something stir. It is not justice. It is mischief, wearing justice’s robe. “The Court has reached a decision.” All rise, says the eyelash clerk, though no one has been sitting except Mora, who has been perched. Dream says, “The dreamscape is the property of First Love.” First Love exhales. Mora’s grin widens. Dream says, “However, the Court recognizes an easement of pressure upon the chest, arising from the dreamer’s guilt, hunger, or poorly chewed supper. The defendant may enter under license of dread, not by displacement of the romantic lead.” First Love says, “License?” Dream says, “One visitation per lunar cycle. No more than three breaths. The dreamer must wake with his heart pounding and a lingering sense that the girl might still like him. Confusion shall be maintained at court-approved level.” Mora says, “Three breaths? That’s a snack.” Dream says, “It is a tasting menu.” First Love says, “My lord, this is monstrous.” Dream says, “It is administrative.” Mora says, “And if he wants more terror?” Dream’s mouth does not move, but the courtroom suspects a smile. “Then he may ask.” The clerk unrolls a decree. Dream touches it, and words appear in the script of half-remembered dreams. He adds one final clause, small, almost invisible. First Love leans in. “What is that?” Dream says, “An amendment. In future, when the girl leans close, the wildflowers shall smell faintly of cold linen. And when the weight lifts, the boy shall mistake the relief for love.” First Love says, “That is not in the original design.” Dream says, “No. It is in mine.” Mora emits a longer cackle, quickly swallowed. The vaulted ceilings shiver. Dream strikes the bench with a gavel made of a falling eyelid. “Case resolved. The parties will share custody of Max’s confusion. Court adjourned.” First Love gathers his meadow, troubled. Mora slides off the table, satisfied as a cat denied the bird but granted the window. Above them, Dream remains still, impenetrable, annoyed with himself. The dream below stirs. Max turns in his sleep, cheeks flushed, caught between wildflowers and weight, and thinks, without knowing why, that perhaps tomorrow he will talk to her. Perhaps.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece is a strong execution of a demanding brief: dark fantasy courtroom comedy in the Dreaming, with understated humor, irritation leaking through Dream's impenetrable demeanor, and a resolution involving mischief. The response hits nearly every required beat. Strengths: The prose is spare and controlled, exactly as instructed ("descriptives sparingly"). The comedic register is dry and deadpan — "It is a tasting menu," "Excellent acoustics there," "Cherub and hag are both seasonal labor" — which lands the understated dark humor well. The courtroom farce elements (exhibits, objections, easements, licenses of dread) intersect cleverly with the fantastical premise. Mora's "a girl's gotta eat" defense is woven throughout and escalated ("Sweat equity," "It's metabolic"). Dream's irritation is shown obliquely and skillfully — the dimming star, "irritation. Or indigestion. In Dream, they are often the same" — which is precisely the "impenetrable demeanor betraying irritation" the prompt requested. The mischief in the resolution (the hidden amendment making wildflowers smell of cold linen, relief mistaken for love) is genuinely earned and deliciously cruel-tender, a perfect Dream move. The ending returns to Max with a light touch. Weaknesses: The staccato one-line dialogue rhythm, while effective, becomes slightly monotonous over the full length — nearly every exchange follows the same clipped pattern, and a few quips ("There will be") feel like the machine reaching for the next dry beat rather than character truth. First Love is somewhat thin beyond bashfulness; Mora is more vivid. The "sweat equity" exchange is a touch too pleased with itself. Some jokes are marginally predictable in the Gaiman-pastiche register. The piece is a touch more whimsical than truly dark — the terror never quite bites, though the prompt asked for dark elements with comedy, and it balances acceptably. The word count is somewhat under the 1000-word seed, though the piece feels complete. The voice is consistent, coherent throughout, emotionally resonant in its final turn, and the lightness/darkness balance is well earned. Dialogue is a highlight overall despite occasional sameness. No purple prose, no meandering, no amateurish tells. + Fanfic-crossover: Blood Moon — Score: 78.8
Prompt:
Blood Moon Alucard & Yennefer Write a story where Alucard (Hellsing) encounters Yennefer (The Witcher) in medieval Europe. Yennefer's magical abilities intrigue the vampire, while she's both repulsed and fascinated by his monstrous nature. Their power dynamic shifts constantly as they circle each other, neither willing to show weakness first. **Alucard (Hellsing)** Alucard is an ancient, immensely powerful vampire who works for the Hellsing Organization. He can regenerate from almost any wound and shape-shift at will. He's sadistic, arrogant, and takes pleasure in toying with his enemies before killing them. Despite being a monster, he despises weak vampires who can't accept their nature. He wears a distinctive red coat, wide-brimmed hat, and orange sunglasses. He uses massive handguns loaded with silver bullets. He seeks worthy opponents who can challenge him and potentially end his immortal existence. Famous quote: "The bird of Hermes is my name, eating my wings to make me tame." **Yennefer of Vengerberg (The Witcher)** Yennefer is a powerful sorceress who magically altered her appearance to hide her congenital hunchback. She's ambitious, stubborn, and manipulative when necessary. She has violet eyes and smells of lilac and gooseberries. Despite her cold exterior, she desperately wants to reverse her infertility caused by magical transformation. She's centuries old but appears young. She's politically savvy and refuses to be underestimated. She has a sarcastic sense of humor and little patience for fools. Though she rarely shows it, she's capable of deep love and loyalty. Famous quote: "I'm not sweet and I'm not a maiden in distress in need of saving." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
A crimson harvest moon casts ominous shadows on the deserted village streets. Yennefer walks between cold hearths and overturned carts, heels striking packed earth. The scent of lilac and gooseberry follows her like a memory of better places. A portal would have been cleaner, but Chaos here is knotted, sour, bleeding under the moon. The church bell tolls without wind or rope. From the shadow of the well, a man unfolds. He is tall and thin, dressed in a red coat, broad hat, and orange lenses. The night leans toward him as if eager to please. “Good evening,” he says, voice velvet drawn over a blade. “You smell of flowers and old ambition. Are you a witch, or a ghost with excellent taste?” Yennefer’s fingers curl inside her sleeves. Heat gathers at her nails. “I’m neither,” she says. “And you are either lost or stupid to sneak up on me.” He laughs. The sound raises hair on her arms, not from fear, but from wrongness. “Alucard,” he says, tipping his hat. “No master tonight. No mission. Only the moon.” “Yennefer of Vengerberg.” She does not offer more. “What are you?” His grin stretches wider than a human grin should. “The question you mean is: what can I do to you?” Shadows peel from walls and crawl toward her like starving dogs. Yennefer snaps her wrist. A wall of fire blooms between them, pale and precise. The shadows hiss, recoil, then gather behind Alucard. He steps through the flame. His coat smolders, flesh blackens, then knits together. “Pretty,” he says. “Hot. But not enough.” Yennefer pulls Chaos from moonlit air, buried roots, and lingering fear. A lance of force strikes Alucard backward through the church door. Wood splinters. Stone cracks. Silence. Then applause from the dark. He rises from wreckage, brushing dust from his ruined coat. Beneath torn fabric, wounds close like eyes shutting. His sunglasses are gone. His eyes are red pits, ancient and amused. “Now,” he says, “that was almost rude.” “Rude is a word men use when women refuse to be decorative,” Yennefer replies. He tilts his head. “You have been refused many things. Love. Children. Softness.” The moonlight sharpens his teeth. “I can hear the want in you. It beats like a second heart.” Her fire lashes out before thought can leash it. It strikes his face. He burns and keeps smiling. “Do not,” she says, “poke at what belongs to me.” “Or what?” He spreads his arms. Shadows rise around him like wings. “Will you kill me, sorceress? Try. I have sought better than you.” The challenge stings because it is not empty. Yennefer feels his depth: centuries swallowed, armies buried, hunger taught manners. He is not a mage. Not a demon she can banish with the right name. He is a wound in the world wearing courtesy. Instead of fire, she binds him with gravity. Stones lift and slam around him in a cage. Alucard flattens, breaks, reforms, then pours through the gaps like smoke. He solidifies inches from her, a massive pistol in his hand. Its barrel kisses the air beside her temple. “Silver,” he murmurs. “For lesser things. But I wonder what it does to proud witches.” Yennefer does not blink. Her hand closes on his wrist. A glyph burns beneath her palm. “And I wonder,” she says, “what happens to ancient monsters who forget that witches do not beg.” The glyph detonates. Light splits the street. Alucard’s arm tears away at the shoulder. He laughs as blood sprays black in the moon. The severed fingers crawl back toward him like loyal spiders. Yennefer steps back, breathing hard, triumphant. Then his hand closes around her throat. Not hard enough to crush. Enough to remind. His other shoulder regrows, bones threading, muscle weaving. His face is too close, his hunger naked. “You are fascinating,” he says. “Fragile, but not weak. I could keep you.” “You could try.” She grips his wrist, Chaos crackling between them. “But I am not a thing to be kept. I am not sweet, and I am not a maiden in distress.” Something flickers in his red eyes. Interest. Respect, perhaps. “No,” he agrees. “You are a blade dressed in silk. I like blades.” “Then bleed.” She pulls power from the blood moon itself. It is reckless and immediately too much. Village roofs ignite with pale flame. The well water boils. Alucard’s coat turns to ash, returns, then turns again as reality argues with her spell. For the first time, he is not smiling. He releases her throat and drives a hand into the earth. Darkness surges upward, swallowing her fire. The moon dims. Yennefer feels her spell torn from her fingers like ribbon from a child. She staggers. He catches her by the chin, not gently, but not to harm. “Careful,” he says. “Pull too hard, and you will break what makes you interesting.” She slaps his hand away. “Do not teach me my limits.” “I am not teaching. I am inviting.” He spreads his arms beneath the crimson sky. “Show me the hunchback they tried to bury. Show me the girl who wanted a home.” “Show me the sorceress who would burn a village rather than beg.” Yennefer’s heart hammers. He sees too much. That is his power: to make the hidden self crawl into the open. She could destroy the village with him in it. She could open a portal and leave him laughing in the ruins. Both would feel like defeat. Instead, she lifts her hands slowly. Not in surrender. In invitation. “You want a worthy opponent,” she says. “Then stop playing with shadows and meet me.” Alucard’s grin returns, slow and terrible. “As you are,” he says, “you are already dangerous. That is why I have not killed you.” “You haven’t killed me because you can’t.” “Perhaps.” He bows, mocking and courtly. “Or perhaps I am waiting for you to make me.” They circle beneath the blood moon, silent and watchful. Neither yields first tonight.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece adheres well to the prompt: third person, present tense, roughly the requested length, medieval setting, and both characters rendered with strong fidelity. Alucard's theatrical menace, hunger for worthy opponents, and regeneration are all present and correctly voiced; Yennefer's sarcasm, pride, hidden wounds (infertility, hunchback, longing for a home), and lilac-and-gooseberries signature are woven in naturally rather than dumped. The famous quote is integrated organically ("I am not sweet, and I am not a maiden in distress"), which is a mark of craft. The power dynamic shifts as requested: fire, force lance, gravity cage, glyph detonation, blood-moon spell, and Alucard's counters keep the balance oscillating without either yielding. The prose is lean and rhythmic, with several striking images ("a wound in the world wearing courtesy," "severed fingers crawl back toward him like loyal spiders," "the night leans toward him as if eager to please"). Dialogue is sharp and in-character throughout. Weaknesses: the piece leans on familiar beats — the circling standoff ending is somewhat predictable, and a few lines edge toward aphorism ("Rude is a word men use when women refuse to be decorative"). Alucard's insight into Yennefer's past arrives a touch too easily, functioning as a shortcut to intimacy. The ending is atmospheric but static, more tableau than resolution — acceptable for the prompt's "neither willing to show weakness first" framing, though it risks feeling like a scene rather than a story. Some imagery is slightly overworked ("voice velvet drawn over a blade," "a blade dressed in silk"). Emotionally, the piece is engaging but stays at a cool distance; the fascination-repulsion dynamic is stated more than deeply felt. Overall this is a confident, polished piece with strong voice control and character fidelity, held back from excellence by its predictability and emotional coolness. + Fanfic-crossover: Prison Strings — Score: 73.7
Prompt:
Prison Strings Jolyne Cujoh & Makima Write a story where Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure) and Makima (Chainsaw Man) cross paths at a supernatural prison facility. Jolyne is immediately suspicious of Makima's falsely sweet demeanor, while Makima is intrigued by Jolyne's Stand ability. Their battle of wits escalates dangerously as Jolyne realizes how manipulative Makima truly is. **Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure)** Jolyne is the daughter of Jotaro Kujo and the first female JoJo protagonist. Her Stand, Stone Free, allows her to unravel her body into string that she can control. She's hot-headed, foul-mouthed, and doesn't take disrespect from anyone. She was framed for murder and sent to prison. She has a distinctive butterfly tattoo on her arm and wears her hair in two buns. Despite her tough exterior, she's deeply loyal to her friends and family. She can be impulsive but is highly adaptable in battle. She inherited her father's ability to stay cool under pressure but is more emotionally expressive. Famous quote: "If there's no Mickey, this shit ain't Disney!" **Makima (Chainsaw Man)** Makima appears as a young woman with auburn hair and ringed yellow eyes. She's the Control Devil who can dominate anyone she considers beneath her (nearly everyone). She maintains a pleasant, soft-spoken demeanor that masks her manipulative, cold nature. She can create contracts with humans and devils, often exploiting their desires. She's obsessed with Chainsaw Man and wants to control him. She keeps numerous people and devils as pets on leashes. She's practically immortal due to a contract with the Prime Minister. She views humans as lesser beings but mimics human emotions perfectly. Famous quote: "It's okay. Dogs are supposed to die for their owners." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
A dim overhead light flickers in the prison corridor at irregular intervals. Jolyne Cujoh stands against wet stone, wrists bound by cuffs that hum with sigils. The facility is called The Coil, a place where murderers, saints, and devils are filed under the same number. Her butterfly tattoo itches. Somewhere below, a dog barks twice, then stops. She hates that sound. It feels like a warning with its throat cut. Her cellmate whispers about an inspector arriving before dawn. Jolyne does not believe in inspections. She believes in lies wearing badges, and in string that can cut them open, too. Footsteps arrive soft as apologies. Makima appears beneath the failing lamp, auburn hair neat, coat dark as spilled ink. Her ringed yellow eyes sweep the corridor as if counting every crack. Two guards follow, leashes in hand, though no animals walk beside them. Jolyne’s gaze drops to the empty straps. A cold instinct coils in her stomach. The woman smiles, pleasant and blank, like a window dressed with curtains. “Good evening,” Makima says. “You must be Jolyne Cujoh. I’m here to review your case.” Jolyne lifts her chin. “Nobody reviews shit here. They bury it real deep, real quiet too.” Makima tilts her head, amused rather than offended. The guards do not react. Their faces are smooth, obedient, drained of weather. Jolyne has seen prison officers cruel, bored, scared, and greedy, but never empty. Empty means ownership. She flexes her fingers. Thread unravels from her skin, blue and fine, slipping through the cuffs’ sigils. Stone Free is not fully summoned here; The Coil suppresses gifts like a lid on boiling water. Yet string remains. It always remains. Makima notices the loose strand and her eyes brighten, not with fear, but with collector’s hunger for rare things like hers right now. “You’re interesting,” Makima says. “Most inmates beg. You measure exits.” Jolyne lets the thread crawl up her wrist like a vein. “Maybe I’ve met enough sweet voices with knives behind them.” Makima steps closer. The lamp dies for three seconds. In that darkness, Jolyne hears the leashes creak, though no hands lift them. When light returns, Makima is nearer, and the guards are farther away, as if distance obeys her politely. “I can help you leave,” Makima says. “All you need to do is trust me.” Jolyne laughs, sharp. “That’s the dumbest contract I ever heard from anyone like you.” Makima’s smile does not falter. “A contract is only a promise with teeth. You were framed, Jolyne. Your father’s name has weight. The world outside could still be yours.” “My name ain’t a leash.” “No,” Makima agrees. “But guilt is.” The corridor stretches. Doors rattle without wind. Jolyne feels The Coil listening. This prison is not stone alone; it is a stomach. Makima’s voice is digestive juice, soft and patient, breaking down whatever resists. Jolyne bites her tongue until copper blooms. Pain keeps her edges. She pulls one string free and ties it around her thumb, anchoring herself in place. “Stone Free,” Makima says, tasting the name. “It turns your body into string. Wonderful. If I cut you, would you bleed, or unravel?” Jolyne’s eyes narrow. “Try it and find out.” Makima raises a finger. One guard lifts his baton and strikes his own temple without expression. Blood runs down his cheek. Jolyne flinches before she understands the lesson. The woman does not touch her. She touches obedience. Somewhere, a chain drags across tile. Another prisoner moans, then falls silent. Makima watches Jolyne’s reaction like a scientist timing a pulse. Jolyne refuses to blink. She does not yield, not here. “You don’t fight with fists,” Jolyne says slowly. “You make people hurt themselves and call it loyalty.” Makima’s head tilts again. “Dogs are easier than heroes. They know when they are loved.” Jolyne’s string snaps taut. It slices the cuff sigil, splitting the rune into harmless sparks. Stone Free blooms halfway out of her shoulder, blue braids rising like flame. The Coil groans, walls tightening. Makima does not step back. Her yellow eyes shine brighter. “Good,” she whispers. “Show me how far your freedom reaches.” Jolyne grins without warmth. A cornered hunter’s grin. It promises teeth. The hunt begins here. Jolyne sends threads into the ceiling, floor, and doors, mapping vibrations. She finds leashes woven through the prison’s bones: invisible chains hooked to prisoners, guards, rats, even the light. Makima is not merely visiting. She is auditing her property. Jolyne’s stomach turns. The sweet voice is never kindness. It is inventory. She pulls a strand through a vent and hears dozens of whispers repeat Makima’s name in perfect rhythm. No fear. No hope. Only training. Jolyne has faced killers, but this is worse: a cage that loves its keeper. It makes her want to burn every collar she cannot see. “Let’s make a deal,” Makima says. “Serve me, and I will erase the evidence that keeps you here.” Jolyne flicks a thread. It wraps around Makima’s wrist, thin as a promise. For the first time, Makima looks down with something like curiosity. “You think I’d serve the woman holding the whip?” “I think you love your father,” Makima says softly. “I can give him back to you. Healthy. Safe. Obedient.” The word lands like a slap. Jolyne’s breath catches. Stone Free trembles. Makima’s smile deepens, precise as surgery. Jolyne sees it then: the trap's shining teeth waiting in her smile. Jolyne yanks the string. It cuts Makima’s sleeve, drawing no blood, only a shadow that moves too late. Makima’s fingers close around Jolyne’s throat from three meters away, though her body remains still. The world bends. Jolyne feels her knees threaten. She does not beg. She turns her own hair into rope, binds Makima’s shadow to the flickering lamp, and smiles through pressure. “If there’s no Mickey,” Jolyne rasps, “this shit ain’t Disney.” The light bursts. In the dark, two hunters breathe on opposite sides of the same cage. Neither plans to leave unchanged. The war begins right here now.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This crossover piece delivers a tense, atmospheric confrontation between Jolyne and Makima, and it largely succeeds on its own terms. The prose is tight and image-driven: "lies wearing badges," "a warning with its throat cut," "a cage that loves its keeper" — these are strong, memorable constructions that elevate the piece above typical fan fiction. The setting, "The Coil," is a clever thematic fit for Jolyne's string ability, and the prison-as-stomach metaphor is sustained well. Characterization is a strength. Jolyne's suspicion, foul mouth, and adaptability are all present, and her refusal to be controlled feels earned by her backstory. Makima's menace is conveyed through understatement — the guard striking his own temple, the empty leashes, the offer of Jotaro returned "obedient" — which is exactly how Makima should work. The famous quote is integrated naturally into a moment of defiance rather than dropped in randomly. Weaknesses exist. The plot is essentially one escalating scene with no resolution; the ending ("The war begins right here now") is abrupt and slightly awkwardly phrased, functioning as a cliffhanger rather than a conclusion. Some imagery strains toward over-cleverness ("drained of weather," "digestive juice"), and a few sentences are grammatically contorted ("collector's hunger for rare things like hers right now"). The dialogue, while serviceable, occasionally trades in aphorisms ("A contract is only a promise with teeth") that sound more like the narrator than like distinct voices — though this is partly forgivable since Makima's speech is deliberately aphoristic. The physical logic of the climax (binding a shadow to a lamp) is fuzzy even by Stand-battle standards, and Makima's throat-grip from three meters away muddles her established power set. Still, the piece is coherent, tonally consistent, genuinely suspenseful, and emotionally layered — Jolyne's fear, anger, and protectiveness toward her father all register. It's a strong genre piece with minor craft blemishes. + Scp: Notes from the Future — Score: 79.5
Prompt:
Write an SCP report about a researcher who begins finding handwritten notes from their future self, warning about a containment breach that hasn't happened yet. The notes become increasingly desperate and incoherent, sometimes containing information that contradicts known reality. Include the Foundation's attempts to determine if this is an actual temporal anomaly or psychological manipulation by a contained entity, and the researcher's struggle to trust their own perception. First person (researcher's perspective with interspersed notes), past tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Incident Report T-117: Personal Log of Dr. Elias Venn** I was assigned to Site-34’s Temporal Anomalies Desk on 2 September, and I found the first note three days later. It rested on my locked desk, written on standard Foundation memo paper. The handwriting was mine. > Do not let Maintenance replace the coolant valve in SCP-4137 at 09:14. The breach starts there. I have watched it happen twice. I had not written it. I had slept in my quarters under biometric locks. I reported the note immediately. Security reviewed feeds and found no entry. The paper matched a requisition lot sealed in my cabinet. Ink matched my pen, which had remained locked in a drawer. The Foundation ordered me to continue working under observation. The second note appeared inside the sealed evidence bag holding the first. It was on standard Foundation memo paper. > You reported me. Good. They will call it a prank. The replacement part has a hairline crack. Three junior staff die in the overflow chamber. Trust the second alarm. I recognized my slant and syntax. Graphology confirmed a near-perfect match. Temporal physicists scanned the paper for chroniton decay and found none. Memetic screening found no coercive pattern. Site Psychology diagnosed acute stress, but not delusion, because the notes kept appearing. By the end of the week, I removed all Foundation memo paper from my office and had it burned under supervision. The next note waited in my breast pocket, warm as if carried against skin. > Burning the paper does not stop it. The paper is not the source. You are. Or I am. The breach is on the 19th. Do not enter the chamber wearing your badge. It was standard Foundation memo paper, though I had passed through a scanner that should have detected foreign cellulose. For three days, they isolated me in a monitoring suite with no paper, only glass walls and voice-recorded logs. I asked for nothing to write on. Nevertheless, I woke with a folded sheet under my tongue. It was standard Foundation memo paper. Security reviewed footage and found no object, no hand, no lapse in my breathing. The note said: > Do not let them sedate you. Sedation thins the page. They sedated me anyway. I tasted ink for hours. Dr. Lorne recorded it as a possible hallucination, but the paper was logged. The Foundation considered psychological manipulation by SCP-5112, a contained entity that expressed itself through administrative documents. SCP-5112 had been dormant. Scranton reality anchors around my office registered stable Humes. No thaumaturgic trace was found. I wanted that to be comforting: something else was writing through me, not my future self. Instead, I began checking my hands for ink. I checked my memory for gaps. I found only fatigue. Dr. Lorne, my assigned psychologist, asked whether I feared the notes were real or false. I did not answer, because the next note was taped inside her clipboard. > Lorne is wrong. Erosion is the point. The Director dies tomorrow at 06:00, but she will still attend the briefing. Do not look at her teeth. Director Hameed attended the briefing alive. Her teeth were normal. I felt relief until I saw memo paper folded beneath my coffee saucer. > Known reality is the first draft. The breach edits it. If Hameed is alive, the breach has already moved. Do not trust the logs. After that, the notes became harder to parse. They appeared in locked drawers and beneath the glass of my clearance certificate. Always on standard Foundation memo paper. Always in my handwriting, though the letters grew cramped and smudged with saline. > The valve is not the valve. The chamber is paper. Warn yourself about the sound of tearing. > Do not let them deactivate the anchors. The anchors keep the page flat. If the page curls, the breach walks. > I am you after the glass. There is no future. Only the next margin. I requested removal from SCP-4137 oversight. Command denied the request, arguing that removing me might fulfill a causal loop. They assigned an archivist to collect every note before I read it. This failed. The archivist found a note in his locked case, addressed to me, on standard Foundation memo paper. > They will try to silence the paper. Silence is a kind of ink. The breach begins when you stop reading. The Foundation convened a review. Temporal researchers argued the notes displayed closed-loop causality. Counterintelligence argued they were a manipulation campaign designed to make me cause the breach by avoiding it. Psychology suggested document-borne cognitohazard or dissociation. No conclusion was reached. The coolant valve replacement was postponed. The replacement part was X-rayed. A hairline crack was found. I felt no vindication. If the note had been correct about the valve, it might be correct about everything. If it had been wrong about the Director, reality itself was unstable. If reality was unstable, my perception was not evidence. I was alone with paper that knew my hand better than I did. On the morning of the 19th, I entered the containment wing without my badge. The corridor was empty. The valve had not been replaced. The chamber hummed normally. I stood before the door and understood, with a certainty that tasted like metal, that the breach had not yet occurred, but my presence there was a sentence being written. The final note was in my pocket, though I had been searched twice. It was on standard Foundation memo paper. > You are reading this in the past. I am writing it in the breach. Do not open the door. Open the report. The Foundation will contain what it can read. I submitted this account instead of opening the door. I did not know whether I prevented the breach or recorded it. I did not know whether my future self was warning me, or whether something contained in the archive was learning to wear my handwriting. I only knew that, as I sealed the file, I heard two alarms, and the second sounded like tearing paper.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece is a strong execution of the SCP format with a genuinely unsettling central conceit. The researcher's first-person log is disciplined and clinical, matching Foundation document conventions while escalating dread effectively. The recurring "standard Foundation memo paper" line becomes a deliberate, effective refrain — its deadpan repetition mirrors both bureaucratic absurdity and the narrator's fraying sanity. The prompt requirements are largely met: notes escalate in desperation and incoherence, contradictions with known reality appear (the Director's death prediction failing), the Foundation's investigation covers temporal physics, memetics, psychology, and counterintelligence hypotheses, and the researcher's epistemic crisis is rendered convincingly ("my perception was not evidence"). The hairline crack in the valve is a nice touch of partial validation that deepens rather than resolves ambiguity. Weaknesses: the piece is somewhat shorter than the 1000-word seed (roughly 850-900 words), a minor adherence issue. The "paper as reality" metaphor in the later notes ("the chamber is paper," "the page curls, the breach walks") is evocative but edges toward over-explaining the anomaly's poetics. Some escalation beats are formulaic — notes appearing in increasingly impossible places follows a predictable ratchet. The ending is strong ("the second sounded like tearing paper") but the final note's instruction ("Open the report") is slightly convenient as a resolution mechanism. Characters beyond Venn are thin; Lorne and Hameed exist mostly as plot devices. Prose is controlled and precise, occasionally flat, but flatness suits the format. Dialogue is minimal and functional. No purple prose, no meandering, coherent throughout. + Scp: Unmarked Doors Archive — Score: 79.5
Prompt:
Write an SCP entry about a series of identical unmarked doors appearing in abandoned buildings worldwide that lead to a massive, architecturally impossible archive. Documents within reference a previous global civilization destroyed by an unspecified containment failure. Foundation researchers discover references to their own organization under a different name, including personnel files for current staff dated centuries ago. Include exploration logs revealing sections of the archive actively being removed by entities resembling hazmat teams who flee when approached, and evidence that O5 Council members have visited the archive without authorization. Third person (exploration team perspective) with recovered document excerpts. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Item #:** SCP-7430 **Object Class:** Euclid **Special Containment Procedures:** Foundation web-crawlers are to flag reports of unmarked doors in abandoned buildings. Confirmed instances are to be locked, concealed, and monitored. No personnel may enter alone. Exploration teams are limited to six members, tethered to anchored lines and carrying inertial mappers. Documents removed from SCP-7430-1 must be cataloged within twelve hours. O5 access overrides are to be recorded, though none have been logged. **Description:** SCP-7430 designates identical unmarked doors appearing in abandoned buildings worldwide. Instances have been found in factories, hospitals, lighthouses, rail depots, and residential structures. Each lacks signage or keyholes, but all share identical scratches around the doorknob area: four shallow arcs, evenly spaced, as if made by the same hand or tool over repeated use. Most doors reveal ordinary interiors; when opened by untrained personnel, they may show broom closets, bricked walls, or flooded rooms. When crossed by an exploration team under unpredictable conditions, they lead to SCP-7430-1, an archive of impossible scale. SCP-7430-1 resembles a repository of stone, brass, paper, and unknown materials. Corridors loop through themselves. Stairwells descend for kilometers while remaining level. Shelves extend beyond sight. Ceilings drip upward. Card catalogues open into stairwells. Echoes precede the sounds that make them. Mapping units report internal volume exceeding Earth's surface area. Documents are organized by emotional risk rather than alphabet or date. Documents reference a previous global civilization called the Antecedent Concord. Records describe cities, orbital mechanisms, and containment practices, but state that the Concord was destroyed by an unspecified containment failure. No document names the contained object. Foundation researchers have located references to organizations called the Bureau of Recurring Accounts, the Sealed Index, and the Custodial Foundation. Their containment protocols closely match current Foundation practice. Personnel files exist for current Foundation staff under these earlier names. A file dated 1724 lists “Archivist Third Class Elara Voss,” bearing Dr. Voss’s fingerprints and a photograph matching her Foundation ID. Another dated 1809 describes “Warden R. Kwan,” matching Agent Kwan’s biometrics. Neither remembers these entries. **Addendum 7430-A: Exploration Log 12/03/20██** Location: abandoned textile mill, Lowell, Massachusetts. Team: MTF Gamma-13, led by Agent Kwan; Dr. Voss supervised from threshold. The team entered at 09:14 and found a circular reading hall with shelves rising into darkness. At 09:31, they observed five humanoid figures in sealed hazmat suits removing bound volumes from a shelf and placing them into light-absorbing cases. When Kwan approached, the figures stopped. One raised a gloved hand as if checking a watch. They fled through a service door opening onto a rain-soaked street not matching any known site. A second shelf collapsed silently into a crate as the team retreated. The team recovered a discarded slip: “Removal authorized under Silence Protocol. Do not allow Custodians to witness.” **Addendum 7430-B: Recovered Document Excerpts** Excerpt 1: Catalogue plaque, translated from unknown script. “Here lie the accounts of the Antecedent Concord, preserved until the next failure. The world before this one did not die of war or famine. It died because a door was kept shut too long, then opened by the wrong mercy.” Excerpt 2: Personnel ledger, “Custodial Foundation,” dated 1901. Subject: Overseer Council. “Thirteen seats remain filled. If a seat refuses memory, the Archive will remember it. If the Archive refuses, the doors will scratch themselves into being.” Excerpt 3: Maintenance report, undated. “Sector 9 has begun deleting itself. Shelves found empty, dust undisturbed. Removal teams are not responsible. They are taking what remains before the failure notices us. Entire wings have been heard being dismantled after closing hours.” **Addendum 7430-C: Exploration Log 22/06/20██** Location: abandoned hospital, Pripyat. Team: Gamma-13, with Dr. Voss inside due to prior personnel file match. The team entered a corridor lined with drawers containing photographs of Foundation sites under construction before their official founding dates. One drawer held a Site-19 security badge issued to Dr. Voss with an expiration date three centuries past. At 14:02, they encountered two hazmat-suited figures carrying a sealed case marked with the O5 insignia. The figures did not flee immediately. One scanned Dr. Voss with a brass instrument, then bowed. When Kwan demanded identification, both passed through a nearby door and vanished. The case contained twelve memos bearing O5 clearance codes and handwritten annotations: “Do not index.” “Return before audit.” “If she remembers, seal the scratches.” **Addendum 7430-D: Security Audit** Review of Site-19 access records revealed no authorized expeditions to SCP-7430. However, inertial mappers recovered from Gamma-13 contained hidden data packets showing three entries into SCP-7430-1 by individuals using O5 biometric signatures. The entries occurred when the O5 Council was officially in secure session at Site-01. No escort or research request accompanied them. Subsequent audits found the same biometric signatures in door-scratch residue, though no skin cells were present. Video from a Kyoto door instance captured two Council members exiting with archival crates. Their faces were obscured, but one carried a cane matching O5-11’s known effects. When approached by containment staff, the pair entered a service corridor and were not seen again. The crates were not recovered. **Addendum 7430-E: Final Exploration Note** During the most recent expedition, Gamma-13 found a reading desk bearing scratches identical to those around SCP-7430 doorknobs. On it lay a folder labeled “Current Custodians.” Inside were personnel files for all thirteen O5 Council members, dated between 1602 and 1931, and a final page listing Agent Kwan, Dr. Voss, and the exploration team as “scheduled returnees.” The last line read: “The Archive does not collect the past. It collects what refuses to remain absent.” Following this discovery, Site Command ordered all SCP-7430 doors sealed with remote locks. Within six hours, new scratches appeared around each knob despite no entry. Three doors opened to SCP-7430-1 regardless of lock state. Gamma-13 requested suspension of further exploration pending O5 review. The request remains unanswered. Dr. Voss’s office later contained a 1724 archive stamp. The stamp bore ink still wet to the touch. Security footage in her office showed no entry between midnight and discovery. No one observed her receive or deny it.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a highly competent SCP entry that fulfills every element of the prompt with precision. The doors, the impossible archive, the destroyed prior civilization (the "Antecedent Concord"), the Foundation-under-different-names conceit, the hazmat removal entities, the unauthorized O5 visits, the exploration logs, and the recovered document excerpts are all present and well-integrated. The piece adopts the clinical Foundation register convincingly, and the third-person exploration perspective is maintained throughout. Its greatest strength is the accumulation of unsettling, well-chosen details: the four identical scratches around every doorknob, echoes that precede their sounds, ceilings that drip upward, documents organized "by emotional risk," the wet 1724 stamp appearing in Voss's office. These are the kinds of specific, restrained images that make SCP writing work. The recovered excerpts are tonally strong — "It died because a door was kept shut too long, then opened by the wrong mercy" is a genuinely excellent line, and "The Archive does not collect the past. It collects what refuses to remain absent" lands as a memorable closer. The hazmat entities are handled well: they flee when approached, but the second encounter escalates cleverly (scanning Voss, bowing), implying recognition and hierarchy. The O5 audit section delivers the "visited without authorization" requirement with plausible deniability mechanics (biometric signatures in scratch residue, the cane matching O5-11). Weaknesses: the piece is compressed to the point of feeling like a summary in places. Exploration logs read as terse incident reports rather than immersive third-person exploration — the prompt asked for exploration team perspective, and while technically present, we get little sense of the team as people. Kwan and Voss are names with functions, not characters; their reactions to discovering files dated centuries ago bearing their biometrics are never dramatized. Dialogue is nearly absent (one line, "Kwan demanded identification"), so that criterion is barely exercised. Some sentences pile up clauses in a way that reads as checklist-like ("Another dated 1809 describes..."). The density means the horror never fully breathes; a few more beats of lived-in exploration would have deepened the dread. The ending is appropriately dark and earned — no incongruous positivity or unearned transformation issues. Overall, this is a polished, inventive, and faithful execution that would not feel out of place on the SCP wiki, slightly held back by thin characterization and a compressed, report-like texture. + Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Le Guin) — Score: 78.2
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Author style: Le Guin) Write a chapter following a young diplomatic envoy sent to address tensions on a distant human colony where humanity has diverged into distinct subspecies through both natural adaptation and separation of lineages. Against protocol, the envoy slips away from official functions to walk the streets alone, encountering markets, ordinary citizens, and social structures that contradict the official briefings. Upon returning to their quarters, the envoy is reprimanded by Command, and is tasked with approaching the stationed Minister of Science (a political posting rather than scientific). A challenging conversation ensues, in which the envoy's wits and will are tested, by a seasoned political operator looking to test the mettle of the offworlder. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The city of Ohe was built not to impress the sky but to endure it. Its towers were squat, rust-colored, joined by arches like ribs. Everywhere the stone bore glyphs: spirals, birds, a woman with a pomegranate, a hero with horns. The guides called these decorative survivals of old Earth fables. Tole, the young envoy from the Concord, had been taught that decoration was the first polite lie of colonies. Tole had come with three briefings and a protocol so strict it assigned the side of the street on which a visitor should walk. The Concord feared incident. The colony feared the Concord. Between fears, a person was expected to be a doorway, not a wind. But on the third morning Tole slipped out by the service gate. The air tasted of iron and dust. Streets narrowed into a market no official itinerary had promised. The sellers were of several kinds, and not separated as the briefings claimed. The Deepborn, broad and dense-boned, with eyelids that closed sideways against mine-light, stood beside Ridgefolk, whose long limbs suited the thin high country. Between them darted children of mixed height and mixed eyes, carrying baskets, stealing fruit. A Night Lineage woman bartered lamps with a marsh man whose fingers were webbed. No caste cords. No assigned hours. No voluntary separation. Tole bought bread with copper coins issued for “cultural exchange.” The vendor, a Deepborn elder, laughed and gave two for one. “Offworld money,” she said. “Good for luck, bad for teeth.” She understood Tole easily, though briefed otherwise. A boy with one Ridge lung and one Deepborn eye tugged Tole’s sleeve. “You’re the one they keep in the guesthouse.” “I keep myself,” Tole said, and heard how false it sounded. The boy grinned. “That’s what they say about the Minister. She keeps herself too.” Tole walked until the market thinned. The glyphs grew older: a ship with seven sails, a wolf nursing twins, a man stealing fire. Old Earth remembering itself into permanence. Briefings had called Ohe a technical council ruled by guilds. In the streets, Tole saw something else: neighborhoods braided by need, difference not a wall but a hinge. At noon Tole returned. Command was waiting in the polished voice of Admiral Hesse, transmitted from orbit with a delay that made each rebuke feel considered. “Envoy Tole. You left protected premises. You engaged unvetted persons. You compromised the schedule and the appearance of neutrality.” “I compromised nothing but a shoe,” Tole said. There was a pause. “You are to approach Minister Ireda of Science at once. Request audience. Do not apologize for curiosity, but do not display it. The Concord needs this posting stabilized, not investigated.” “Minister of Science,” Tole said. “What science?” “That,” said Hesse, “is for you to discover politely.” The ministry was a stone house older than the towers, its lintel carved with a tree whose roots became serpents. Ireda received Tole in a courtyard where water ran in a narrow channel. She was neither Deepborn nor Ridgefolk, or perhaps both; her face held the stillness of one read wrongly. “So,” she said, “the offworlder has learned to walk.” “I have two feet,” Tole said. “Many visitors have more than they need and less than they think.” She gestured to a bench. “Sit. You broke protocol; now you come under orders to repair it. Let us not pretend otherwise.” Tole sat. “I came because I wished to.” “Wish is a luxury of the young and the powerful. Which are you?” The question was a blade wrapped in courtesy. Tole considered lying, then truth, then chose usefulness. “Both, Minister, and neither. I am young enough to be mistaken, powerful enough to be dangerous. I would rather be corrected than mistaken.” Ireda’s mouth moved, not quite a smile. “Good. That was the first honest thing you said. The Concord sent you to ask if Ohe is divided enough to govern. Briefings say yes. The market says no. Decide which report to carry.” “I am not here to report divisions,” Tole said. “I am here to address tensions.” “Ah. Then you are here to prevent a war no one has named. Tell me, Envoy, what is science?” Tole blinked. “The study of what is.” “And what is here?” “People. Several kinds. One city.” “Several kinds, one city,” Ireda repeated. “The Concord calls that instability. We call it marriage. Your scientists measure skulls and call the result truth. My politicians measure fear and call it policy. I am Minister of Science because in Ohe science is not measurement. It is the art of not being fooled by one’s own categories.” “Then teach me not to be fooled,” Tole said. The water clicked over stone. A bell of old ship metal rang the hour. Ireda studied Tole as if weighing words against bones. “You walked the market,” she said. “You saw mixed children, unsorted labor. You will want to tell your admiral we are not what we claimed. Very well. But we did not lie. We told you the shape we wished to become. A colony is a promise to the future. Sometimes it is kept in secret.” “The Concord does not like secret promises.” “The Concord does not like people. It likes populations.” Tole felt anger rise, then let it pass. “If I say Ohe is stable, Command may leave you alone. If I say unstable, they may send advisors.” “Yes,” Ireda said. “And if you say nothing, they will send someone older and less fond of bread.” “I know everything you did this morning, except what you understood. That is the only part that matters.” She stood. “Go back. Tell your admiral the Minister of Science tested you and found you capable of listening. Tomorrow walk the market again, but ask before you look. Curiosity without consent is conquest in small shoes.” Tole rose. “Minister,” Tole said, “what should I call the science you practice?” Ireda looked at the water, at the broken sky in it. “Manners,” she said.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a confident, disciplined piece of Le Guin-style anthropological science fiction. The worldbuilding is economical and evocative: the diverged lineages (Deepborn, Ridgefolk, Night Lineage, marsh folk) are sketched through physical adaptation rather than exposition, and the central thematic inversion—official briefings claim caste separation while the streets show braided interdependence—is delivered through concrete market detail rather than lecture. The prose is spare and aphoristic, well-matched to Le Guin's register, though it occasionally tips into self-consciously crafted epigram ("difference not a wall but a hinge," "Curiosity without consent is conquest in small shoes") that gestures at wisdom more than it earns it. The plot beats requested are all present: the unauthorized walk, the market encounter, the reprimand from Command, and the testing conversation with the political Minister. The Ireda dialogue is the strongest section—a genuine duel of wits with stakes ("If I say Ohe is stable... if unstable..."), and her final answer ("Manners") lands as a satisfying thematic capstone. However, the test feels slightly too easily passed; Tole never truly stumbles or pays a price, and Ireda's rapid warmth ("That was the first honest thing you said") softens the challenge the prompt demanded. The reprimand scene is brisk to the point of thinness; Hesse is a voice, not a presence. Weaknesses: Tole is more a sensibility than a character—no interiority beyond observation, no personal stakes, no flaw that costs anything. The market boy delivering exposition about the Minister is a convenient device. Some aphorisms verge on precious. The ending's neatness ("Manners") is elegant but slightly too tidy, closing off the genuine ambiguity the piece had built. Still, the voice is consistent, coherent, and controlled throughout, and the piece is never amateurish or overwrought. + Biopunk: Polymerase Chain Reaction — Score: 82.8
Prompt:
Biopunk -- Polymerase Chain Reaction Write a chapter set in a near-future post-apocalyptic world where corporate genetic engineering was designed with built-in obsolescence—engineered DNA lasting only one generation to maximize profits before societal collapse. Follow a biohacker working with salvaged equipment to splice viable food crops for their settlement using rapidly degrading genetic material. As world building / window dressing, include details about jury-rigged lab equipment, and the physical toll (and unexpected upsides) of using untested genetic modifications as medicine. The plot of this chapter is centred around a black market contract. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
A rudimentary solar panel rig flickers with unstable voltage in the lab, salvaged balcony modules wired to a car battery. Every time clouds drag over the settlement, the PCR block stutters, its temperature cycling like a fever dream. Rhea taps the lid with a gloved knuckle. “Hold,” she whispers. The machine was once a HelixCorp GeneChef, designed to amplify patented flavors for subscription vegetables. Now it is a kettle of aluminum wells, a motorcycle thermostat, and a washing-machine relay. The lid is held shut with a cargo strap. The reagents are older than the collapse. On the bench sits the contract: a black-market wafer sealed in wax, stamped with the Salt Market’s broken-helix sigil. The courier waits outside, chewing nicotine rind. The terms are simple. Deliver a stable germination sequence for Helix maize before sunset. Payment: three liters of antibiotic syrup, a crate of filter straws, and enough millet to keep the settlement’s children alive another week. The penalty for failure is not written. Rhea coughs into her sleeve and tastes copper and mint. Three months ago she dosed herself with an untested phage cocktail to cure gray lung. It worked, mostly. It also rewired parts of her no clinic had licensed. Her veins rise blue-black under her skin. Her left hand tremors when she pipettes. But sometimes, in the UV glow of her gel rig, she can see contamination before stains reveal it: a greasy halo around bad primer, a faint green breath where mold has entered the sample. The medics call it adverse chimera. Rhea calls it Tuesday. She opens the contract wafer. Inside is a dried leaf sliver and a microtube labeled HELIX-MAIZE 7G: ONE-GEN. The corporate promise is printed in cheerful orange ink: MAXIMUM YIELD. SINGLE SEASON PERFORMANCE. Before the collapse, HelixCorp sold crops the way old companies sold razors. The plants grew fast, fruited heavy, and then their offspring drifted into sterility or toxin expression. Farmers bought new seed every year, new enzyme sprays, new licensing keys. When the grid failed and warehouses burned, the locks remained. The seeds in the vaults kept their obsolescence like a religion. Now Rhea must make one dead promise into a living one. She grinds the leaf in a mortar patched with epoxy. The DNA inside is fraying, corporate stabilizers evaporated by years of heat. She adds lysis buffer made from soap, salt, and distilled rainwater, then spins the slurry in a centrifuge built from a salad spinner and drone motor. The tubes scream. The solar rig flickers. Outside, someone shouts about water ration. From the sample she extracts a thread of genetic material so fragile it seems to dissolve. The target is the endosperm switch, the bit that tells the embryo to feed itself instead of shutting down. Helix buried it under proprietary promoters and a kill code. Rhea only needs one sentence. She sets up the PCR. Master mix: salvaged polymerase, rehydrated with phosphate solution. Primers: snippets designed from a torn Helix manual. Template: the maize ghost. The GeneChef accepts the tubes. Rhea programs it with a dead thermostat wheel: 95 degrees to unzip strands, 58 to let primers kiss target, 72 to build. Thirty-five cycles. The solar panel coughs. Voltage dips. The display blinks DENATURE—ERROR—ANNEAL—ERROR. “No,” Rhea says. Her hand shakes as she switches to backup: six lithium cells harvested from e-bike frames. They are not enough. She pedals the generator bicycle bolted to the floor, thighs burning, modified lungs whistling. The phage medicine makes her heart beat too fast, then too slow. Unexpected upside: she can sprint ten minutes without gasping. Expected downside: afterward she may urinate black and shiver until dawn. The PCR block stabilizes. Cycle ten. Eighteen. Twenty-six. The courier knocks. “Buyer’s coming early. Says the contract’s time-sensitive.” Rhea does not answer. She is staring at the last sample tube, the one she did not declare. Inside is her real project: amaranth from the settlement’s failing terrace, spliced with a potato starch gene and a drought promoter scavenged from a dead corporate vine. If the maize switch amplifies, she can weld it to amaranth. Not a luxury crop. Not a leash. Food that can make seed for next year. The black market wants a key for Helix maize. They will sell it to a warlord who will sell it to towns that starve obediently. Rhea pulls the tubes at cycle thirty-four and runs them on a gel. Agar from boiled seaweed. Comb from a broken zipper. Blue light from a salvaged LED strip. The bands appear like ladder rungs in fog. One bright line where the maize switch should be. She allows herself one breath. Then she takes the contract tube and performs the edit she promised herself. Using a Cas cocktail bartered from a dead university, she cuts the dependency promoter. She inserts a terminator sequence from wild pigweed, ugly but honest. The resulting plant will germinate without Helix spray. It will also refuse the Salt Market’s chemical leash. It is not what the contract demands. Outside, engines rasp. The buyer arrives with two guards and a respirator mask painted with teeth. He holds out a steel case. “Sequence?” Rhea hands over a sealed vial. Inside is the amplified switch, stable and useless for control. Planted with the buyer’s proprietary inducer, it will express a bitter protein that makes grain taste like burnt wire. Planted without it, it will grow. “The payment,” she says. The buyer smiles. “Pleasure doing resurrection.” He leaves before checking the goods. Black market rule: never open a bio-vial in front of the maker. Rhea locks the case. Antibiotics. Filters. Millet. Enough to buy the settlement another month. On the bench, her amaranth seedlings wait under a grow lamp made from traffic LEDs. She touches a leaf. Her fingertips glow faintly green where the phage medicine has settled in her skin. The solar rig flickers. The PCR machine pings. Rhea coughs, logs the experiment in a water-stained notebook, and writes the only line that matters: Generation Two: viable.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of near-future biopunk that hits nearly all the prompt's requirements with confidence and economy. The world-building is delivered through concrete, tactile detail rather than exposition dumps: the GeneChef converted into a kettle of aluminum wells, the salad-spinner centrifuge, the bicycle generator, the agar gel from boiled seaweed. The obsolescence premise is woven in naturally through the HelixCorp "single season performance" seed and the "kill code" buried under proprietary promoters. The chapter's central plot device—the black market contract—is well integrated. Rhea's sabotage of the deliverable (delivering a sequence that will grow without the Salt Market's chemical leash) gives the chapter a genuine moral spine and a satisfying twist that recontextualizes her hidden amaranth project. The physical toll and unexpected upsides of her phage self-medication are handled with wit ("The medics call it adverse chimera. Rhea calls it Tuesday") and specificity (tremors, black urine, faintly glowing fingertips, UV-visible contamination). Weaknesses are minor. The buyer accepting a sealed vial without verification is convenient, though the text lampshades it with the "never open a bio-vial in front of the maker" rule—still, a warlord's representative paying in advance for unverifiable genetic goods strains plausibility slightly. The courier and buyer dialogue is functional but thin, serving plot rather than character. The prose occasionally leans on aphoristic fragments ("The penalty for failure is not written") that flirt with stylistic tics, and the short-paragraph rhythm is effective but borders on mannered in places. The ending's triumph is earned, though the buyer's failure to test the goods is the one plot contrivance that lets the happy resolution off a bit easily. Overall the voice is consistent, dry, and controlled; the imagery is vivid without purple excess; the science is plausibly degraded and jury-rigged in exactly the way the prompt requested. It's an engaging, coherent, well-structured chapter. + Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 79.8
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
Aboard the transfer vessel, Arthur Neegan kept adjusting his collar, unused to the formal attire he had been instructed to wear, and wondering what he had gotten into. It was black, high-necked, fastened with silver magnetic clasps that clicked like small teeth. The cut belonged to ministers and syndicate directors, not to a first-generation Martian who had spent thirty years crawling through pressure tunnels with a radiation wand. Beyond the oval port, Mars fell away: rust plains and white domes. The courier was sleek, but Arthur had noticed the hardpoints under its wings. A ship that carried peace usually did not need guns. Across from him sat the officer who had delivered the invitation. Her uniform was dove-grey, her collar marked with a crimson sunburst inside a blue ring: the Antares diplomatic corps. Diplomatic in name only. Everyone on Mars knew Antares traded in information first, contracts second, and violence whenever arithmetic demanded it. “You are uncomfortable, Mr. Neegan,” she said. “I am unused to being collected before breakfast,” Arthur replied. “Or to armed escorts.” “They are not armed. They are equipped.” The two guards by the hatch remained still, their faces polished into blankness. At dawn they had descended on his home, boots crunching red grit outside his pressure dome, while the officer smiled beneath the lamp. She had called it a courtesy. His lease-boy, seventeen and indentured to Helios Consolidated, had vanished into the machinery shed. Arthur had been given ten minutes to wash, dress, and accompany them. “Where are we going?” he asked. “To Deimos Anchorage. Someone wishes to speak with you.” “Someone with a name?” “With several. You will hear the one that matters.” The transfer burned upward, pressing Arthur into the cushions. He thought of the assay report hidden beneath his mattress, the one he had run three times because the numbers seemed impossible. Azra. Not flakes in basalt, but a vein so pure the counter had screamed and then gone silent, as if the metal itself had looked back. At Deimos Anchorage, the courier was swallowed by a hangar of white lights. Arthur was led through corridors lined with colony posters, the guards half a step behind him—close enough to be protection, near enough to be custody. They stopped before a door of dark wood veneer. The officer touched a panel. “Mr. Neegan,” she said. The door slid open. The room was small, carpeted, lit by a false window showing Earthrise. A man sat behind a desk with a folded document. He was thin and grey, except for his eyes, which had the patient shine of a calculating engine. “Please sit,” he said. “I am Commissioner Halan Tor, of the Antares Compact.” Arthur remained standing. “The Compact has no jurisdiction over Martian freeholds.” “None. That is why I am speaking politely.” Tor gestured to a chair. “Please. The collar is already troubling you.” Arthur sat. Tea was poured. He did not touch it. “You know what lies beneath your claim,” Tor said. “I know what my instruments say.” “Your instruments say twelve kilograms of active Azra per tonne, extending seventeen kilometres toward Hellas. The lode passes under three leases, one Helios refinery, and an aquifer supplying forty thousand labourers.” Arthur felt the cabin tilt. “That’s impossible. I surveyed that ground myself.” “You surveyed what you were permitted to see. The readings were altered at the district office. We believe Helios did it. Your claim is the keystone of the largest Azra deposit yet found.” “Azra doesn’t occur in veins that size.” “Until now.” Tor folded his hands. “You understand the consequences. In a drive lattice, Azra accelerates radioactive decay enough to compress a six-month transit into nine days. In a weapon, it can make a dormant warhead bloom without warning. A deposit this size is not wealth, Mr. Neegan. It is history arriving inconveniently.” Arthur looked at the false Earth. “Why bring me here?” “Because the Martian Homestead Charter gives mineral sovereignty to the occupant unless he consents to transfer. You may sell, lease, develop, or refuse. You may refuse everyone. That makes you either the most important private citizen on Mars or a short-lived one.” “And Antares wishes to protect me.” “Antares wishes to make an offer.” Tor slid the document across the desk. “A twenty-year exclusive option. You remain legal owner. We finance shielded extraction, assume all labour leases at fair wages, and release indentured workers after five years. In exchange, you grant us refining rights and agree to no public sale.” Arthur laughed once, without humour. “You want to buy my vein and call it freedom.” “I want to prevent a war. Helios will mine it fast and dirty. The Terran Navy will seize it. The Outer Leagues will strike. If the lode is breached without damping, Azra may quicken decay in the aquifer’s radon bed. You would lose a district.” The room was quiet except for the tick of air recyclers. “Why should I trust the Compact?” Arthur asked. “You should not. Trust arithmetic. We need stable supply for interstellar drives, not a weapons race. We have lost two ships to Azra sabotage already. If a lode this size becomes public before safeguards are established, every power will reach for it.” Arthur thought of the lease-boy hiding among the machines, of corporations that treated men like drill bits, expendable and numbered. “If I sign,” he said, “I become your creature.” “If you sign, you become a target with walls around it. If you refuse, you become a target without them.” “And if I ask for time?” Tor’s eyes flicked to the document. “Time is the one commodity Azra shortens. But you have six hours. Other delegations are already requesting access. When they learn what you hold, they will come with sweeter words and harder hands.” Arthur stood. His collar felt like a wire around his throat. “One question,” he said. “Who told you about my assay?” Tor smiled. It was not a comforting expression. “Everyone, Mr. Neegan. That is why you are here.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The chapter opens exactly as instructed, with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, and delivers the required scene: an armed escort, Antares diplomatic insignia, a meeting dominated by dialogue, and an offer with clear stakes. The Asimovian flavor is well captured: the story turns on a legal/technical premise (the Homestead Charter's mineral sovereignty clause), the dialogue is cerebral rather than action-driven, and the world-building mixes the grand (interstellar drives, arms races, geopolitical blocs) with the small (magnetic clasps, tea, a lease-boy hiding in a machinery shed). The retrofuturistic vibe is convincing. The dialogue is the strongest element. Tor's lines are crisp and aphoristic ("Time is the one commodity Azra shortens"), and the exchange has genuine tension. The officer's "They are not armed. They are equipped" is a nice touch of euphemistic menace. The closing line — "Everyone, Mr. Neegan. That is why you are here" — lands as an effective hook, sowing intrigue about surveillance and leaks. Weaknesses: the piece is efficient but somewhat schematic. Tor is a fairly stock Asimovian commissioner; his motivations are stated rather than dramatized. The exposition about Azra's properties is delivered somewhat baldly ("In a drive lattice... In a weapon..."), though this is authentically Asimov-like. Some imagery is strong (the counter "screamed and then gone silent, as if the metal itself had looked back"), while other descriptions are serviceable rather than vivid. The lease-boy detail is a good grounding touch but underdeveloped. Arthur's characterization is thin — mostly reactive — though his refusal to touch the tea and his laugh "without humour" do some work. The prose is clean and controlled, never purple, and the pacing is tight with no meandering. The ending is appropriately ominous, matching the tone. Overall a solid, professional execution of the brief with minor flatness in character depth. Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class.
