+ Fantasy-humour: Hell is Other Demons — Score: 79.3
Prompt:
Hell is Other Demons Write a day in the life short story. Lucifer morningstar's on again/ off again relationship with Lilith is currently in the "off again" stage, though the cycle may be coming around as Lilith has been stopping by for reasons other than purely violent ones, and Lucifer has been increasingly lonely. Write a day in the life of this power couple, with elements of dark comedy & fantasy. Use understated irony & absurdity by merging the black immorality and everyday business of running hell, against relatable domestic relationship drama. Take cues from Neil Gaiman. 1000 words.
Model Output:
Lucifer Morningstar woke to ash clicking against the bedroom windows like a million tiny clerks demanding signatures. The bed was too wide, a continent of black silk divided into territories: his warm half, her cold half, and the neutral zone where a jade serpent coiled, licking hairs from a brush that had once belonged to Lilith. “Coffee,” the serpent said, in a voice like Lilith thinking about violence. “No,” said Lucifer. “Tea, then. And someone is stealing the Bureau of Minor Agonies.” He rose, put on a dressing gown embroidered with sighs, and poured two cups anyway. One for himself. One for the possibility of her. The ash had fallen since dawn. It fell on the screaming plains, the lava fountains, the flower beds where regret grew in brittle purple petals. In Hell, ash did not dirty; it settled politely on everything, like memory, like management. Lucifer’s morning began with a queue. Demons do not understand queues, but they understand being told they are in one. At his desk, he approved a request to reclassify Mondays as eternal, denied a proposal to torment telemarketers with silence before they spoke, and signed a condolence card to a duke whose favorite torture device had developed anxiety. “Your absence was felt at the Suffering Committee,” said Malphas, his secretary, a raven with a lanyard. “I wasn’t absent,” said Lucifer. “I was thinking.” “That’s worse.” At eleven, Lilith came in without knocking. Knocking was for visitors and repentance. She wore a dress the color of a bruise turning elegant, and ash stood on her shoulders like a second lace. She said she was returning the copper kettle. “You kept it?” Lucifer asked. “I borrowed it.” “In the Ninth Century.” “Time is a lease,” she said. “You default too often.” She set the kettle down. It was older than kingdoms and had once boiled the first soup made by someone who knew what hunger was. Lucifer did not touch it. He did not touch the place on the desk where her shadow fell. They were, by all official circulars, off again. The cycle had seasons: on again, off again, war, famine, the annual argument about whether the River Styx needed lifeguards. Recently, though, she had stopped coming by with daggers. Now she came with questions. Had he fed the basilisk? Had he approved the new complaints form for the damned? Did he think Hell looked tired? He thought Hell looked tired. He thought himself tired. He had begun dusting the guest chair by the window, though no one sat there. At noon they inspected the Circle of Petty Ambition together, because both their names were on the work order. The damned there were required to build glass towers out of their own excuses, then attend meetings about why the towers fell. A soul in a middle-management afterlife tried to hand Lucifer a performance review. Lilith incinerated it with a glance. “Efficient,” said Lucifer. “I was aiming for dramatic,” she said. “Efficiency is what happens when you’re tired.” A demon foreman complained that the Department of Small Betrayals had misplaced its moaning equipment. Lilith listened, asked two questions, and solved the problem by moving a filing cabinet three inches to the left. Lucifer remembered, with a pang like a fork tested against a cracked tooth, that she had always understood the plumbing of despair. “You could delegate,” she said. “I do.” “Not to yourself.” He almost laughed. It came out as a weather event over the Vale of Whispers. Lunch was a working platter: pomegranate seeds, black bread, a jar of ash mistaken repeatedly for salt. They stood at the balcony overlooking the Lake of But Middle Files, where souls paddled canoes through discarded apologies. A pair of lesser demons below were sharing an umbrella against the ash. They were probably in love. Or tax avoidance. Lucifer envied them both. “I heard you canceled the Quarterly Torture Gala,” Lilith said. “Nobody enjoyed it anymore. They just networked.” “You used to enjoy it.” “I used to enjoy many things. Then I learned their names.” She looked at him then, a look that was not soft, because softness in Hell was an ambush. But it had corners. “I stopped by Tuesday,” she said. “I was everywhere.” “You left the lights on in the west tower.” “I was supervising.” “Lucifer.” “The west tower has mood disorders.” “You don’t have to supervise alone,” she said. “That is what underlings are for. And, occasionally, equals.” He wanted to say: Come back. He wanted to say: Leave. He wanted to say: The bed has learned your shape and is threatening to unionize. What he said was, “The kettle scratches the counter.” “I’ll bring a mat,” she said. In the afternoon, he convened the Council of Infernal Revenue. The subject was loneliness, which Hell had recently begun harvesting as a renewable resource. It was in high demand: one drop could make a mortal call an old friend and then put the phone down before they dialed. Lucifer sat through projections of year-on-year yearning, tariffs on unsent letters, the ethical issue of renting out quiet apartments with one chair too few. The council debated whether to market loneliness as luxury or subscription. Lucifer thought of the jade serpent asking for tea. He voted tabled. “Tabled?” said Mammon. “You never table.” “I am expanding the portfolio of silence.” At four, Lilith came back. She said the kettle needed a lid. Lucifer said the lid had been lost in the Fall. She said she had found it under a mountain of unloved apologies. He said, Of course you have. She said, Of course I have. They walked together through the greenhouse of choking flowers, where every petal whispered someone’s last text message. She stopped to straighten a stake around a vine called Maybe Later. He pretended not to notice. He noticed everything. Her wrist was dusted with ash; his fingers itched to brush it away. Instead he brushed a speck from a leaf. The leaf sighed and expired in a small, legal manner. “You’re lonely,” she said. “I’m the Devil.” “That’s a job title.” “It comes with benefits. Dreadful ones.” She plucked a dead flower and tucked it behind his ear. “Wear that. It makes you look less like a monument.” He did not remove it. Dinner was not planned. It became planned. The cook, a disgraced angel with excellent knives, looked from one to the other and produced two plates, then a third, because the jade serpent arrived on schedule and demanded conversation rights. The serpent became a chair, then suggested they all stop pretending to be dignified. They ate in the small kitchen, not the state dining room, because state rooms were for treaties and funerals. Ash fell outside the windows, patient as a queue of apologies. Lilith poured tea from the returned kettle. It did not scratch the counter. She had put a mat beneath it. Afterward, she stood to leave. The cycle was near, he could feel it, the way one feels weather changing in old scars. She paused at the door, one hand on the hinge he had been meaning to fix and she had already fixed. “Tomorrow,” she said, “I’m coming back for the teapot.” “Tomorrow,” he said, “I’ll have it stolen properly.” She smiled, just enough to redraw the geography of his day. The ash fell all night, soft as bureaucracy, gray as beginning. Lucifer did not turn off the west tower lights. He left one of them on, on purpose.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece succeeds admirably at its brief: a Gaiman-inflected day-in-the-life of Lucifer and Lilith, blending domestic comedy with infernal bureaucracy. The understated irony is its chief strength — the ash "settling politely on everything, like memory, like management," the bed "divided into territories," the kettle returned after thirteen centuries. The on/off relationship is rendered through objects (kettle, lid, mat, hinge) rather than declarations, which is the correct Gaiman move. Dialogue is clipped and deflective; Lucifer's inability to say "come back" lands well, and the jade serpent is a charming absurd invention. Weaknesses: the quip density is very high — nearly every line reaches for aphoristic wit, and after a while the cleverness becomes a tic rather than a voice. A few images strain ("a look that was not soft... But it had corners" is muddled rather than pointed). The piece is a touch too long for its idea; the midday sections (loneliness council, greenhouse) somewhat restate what lunch already established, causing mild meandering. The reconciliation arc is subtle and earned via incremental gestures, so the ending's warmth feels congruent, not unearned. The twist-free structure is fine for a slice-of-life, but the piece plays its one card — wry understatement — repeatedly without escalations beyond mild. Still, prose is polished, coherent, tonally consistent, and the emotional undercurrent of loneliness is genuinely affecting beneath the comedy. + Historical fiction: Gladiator — Score: 78.2
Prompt:
Historical Fiction: Write a scene from a story set during the height of the Roman Empire, focusing on a slice of a day in the life of a gladiator. Do not write a combat scene. Use sensory details to capture the sights, sounds, and smells of ancient Rome. Explore the gladiator's thoughts and emotions. The story should also touch on the larger political and social issues of the time period. The piece should feel like a slice of a larger story. First person, past tense, 1000 words.
Model Output:
Before dawn, the bell in the yard had not yet rung, but Rome had begun its restless work. Carts groaned over basalt stones beyond the ludus wall; a donkey brayed; a slave coughed in the corridor. My cell smelled of straw, sweat, vinegar, and the iron tang that never quite left the training sand. I lay still, listening to the breathing of men who slept as if sleep might be taken from them by noon. The city outside was hungry: for bread, for gossip, for games. I knew its appetites because I had become one of them. My name was Cassius, though the trainer called me Cass when he was angry. I had signed my body to the lanista Aemilius Scaurus for three years, not because I loved the arena, but because my father’s debts had become a net around my mother and sister. The law called men like me auctorati, volunteers. The crowd called us infames, shameless things. I called myself alive. A poor citizen could sell his labor to a baker, his voice to a patron, or his blood to the sand. I had chosen the sand because it paid fastest. On the wall beside my pallet hung the weapon I had chosen: a trident with an ash shaft darkened by oil and palms, its three tines uneven, the left one once bent and hammered straight. Below it lay my net, folded like a sleeping bird, weighted with lead rings. I fought as a retiarius, bareheaded, without heavy shield. The murmillos joked that we wore our courage on our faces. The trident had belonged to my father, a fisherman off Ostia, before creditors took his boat. As a boy, I held it in the shallows and felt a promise: steady arms could keep hunger at a distance. When the bell rang, I carried the trident into the yard. Morning light came thin over the porticoes, turning the sand pale gold. The air smelled of dust, lamp oil, and fish-garum porridge stirring in the cookpot. Men emerged blinking: a Gaul with shoulders like an ox yoke, two Syrians whispering in their own tongue, a Dacian boy captured in the northern wars, still soft enough to flinch when the doctore raised his staff. Rome had swallowed provinces and spat them out here, in a training yard, where conquered bodies learned to die in ways that pleased the conquerors. “Corax, you are slow,” the trainer said. He was a freedman with a scar that pulled his mouth sideways. I planted the trident’s butt in the sand and began my footwork. Step, turn, cast. The net left my hand with a whisper and settled over the wooden post. I pulled it back, gathered the weights, and cast again. Around me, wooden swords clacked against posts, feet thudded, breath rasped. No one spoke of the coming games, but they were in every silence. Caesar Trajan would return from Dacia with gold, captives, and a need to make the city love him more than it feared him. Before midday, Aemilius arrived with a secretary bearing wax tablets and a senator’s freedman in fine wool. The freedman inspected us as a buyer inspects horses. “My patron wishes fighters who can please the crowd without dying too quickly,” he said. The trainer spat. “Dying quickly is cheap. Living well is expensive.” I kept casting my net. Rome was a city of owners. Some owned grain ships from Egypt, some owned votes in the Senate. Men like Aemilius owned our labor. Men like the patron owned Aemilius, in all but name. At midday we ate barley porridge, onions, and watered wine. I sat against the colonnade, where the stone was warm. The Dacian boy sat near me, nursing a blistered hand. He could not have been more than sixteen. His people had been beaten into the empire so that Caesar could parade their gold through Roman streets. I gave him a piece of onion. He stared at it as if it were a test, then ate. “You speak Latin?” I asked. “A little.” “Learn more,” I said. “It will not save you, but it will let you choose your silence.” In the afternoon, the doctore allowed us to oil our bodies and scrape them with strigils. The oil was cheap, sharp with perfume, but the ritual steadied me. I cleaned the trident with a rag, rubbing the shaft where my father’s hands had once rested. The left tine had a small notch. I remembered every time it had been bent, not because of violence, but because of the days after: the physician’s vinegar wash, a coin pressed into my palm by a woman who believed my survival had cured her child’s fever. A messenger boy came at dusk with a bronze disc stamped with Aemilius’s seal. It meant I had been chosen for the preliminary procession at the amphitheatre. It did not mean I would fight, or live. It meant only that my name had passed from one tablet to another. I stood in the yard as the sky turned bronze. From the city came smells of bakeries, dung, incense from a shrine to Fortuna. Somewhere beyond the walls, my mother sold baskets in the Subura. My sister copied letters for a scribe. I had promised them I would buy back our family’s name. I lifted the trident and felt its balance, the slight pull toward the repaired tine. It was not a noble weapon. Senators preferred swords, the legion’s iron argument. But the trident had three points, and I had three reasons to survive: my mother, my sister, and the stubborn hope that Rome, for all its hunger, might one day let a man walk out of its shadow with his face uncovered. The bell rang again, low and final. I leaned the trident against the wall and went to eat the evening bread. It was dark, gritty, and warm. Above the barracks, stars appeared over the city of marble and mud, empire and appetite.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a disciplined, well-researched slice-of-life narrative that fulfills nearly all prompt requirements: first person, past tense, roughly 1000 words, no combat scene, rich sensory detail, interiority, and clear engagement with Roman social/political realities (auctorati status, infamia, debt, provincial conquest, patron-client dynamics, Trajan's Dacian wars). The historical texture is convincing and specific — the retiarius equipment, the lanista, the garum porridge, the strigils, the bronze disc summons. Strengths: The prose is controlled and economical, with a consistent melancholy, pragmatic voice. The trident as inherited object linking fisherman father to gladiator son is a well-integrated symbol rather than a heavy-handed one. The Dacian boy scene is the emotional core and earns its quiet moment ("It will not save you, but it will let you choose your silence" is the best line in the piece). The social commentary is woven into observation rather than lectured, mostly. The ending's "marble and mud, empire and appetite" is a strong closing cadence. Weaknesses: The piece occasionally tips into aphorism-overload — "Rome was a city of owners," "I knew its appetites because I had become one of them," "Dying quickly is cheap. Living well is expensive." These are quotable but slightly writerly, telling us the theme rather than letting it emerge. The political commentary, while integrated, is somewhat familiar territory (empire as appetite, conquered bodies entertaining conquerors) — competent but not surprising. The dialogue is functional but thin; the trainer's lines are stock-gruff. The Dacian boy is a type (innocent conquered youth) more than a person. The narrative arc is deliberately flat — appropriate for a slice-of-life, but it means the piece coasts on atmosphere rather than building tension; the summons disc introduces mild stakes that are immediately deflated by the narrator's own commentary. Some metaphors are near-misses: the net "folded like a sleeping bird" is pretty but slightly precious; "the legion's iron argument" is clever but showy. No purple prose, no meandering, no amateurish errors, no unearned transformations (none occur), ending tone is appropriately bittersweet rather than falsely positive. It is a very good professional-quality piece that stops short of distinction: it executes the assignment rather than transcending it. + Epistolary: The Lighthouse Keeper — Score: 86.6
Prompt:
The Lighthouse Keeper Epistolary Narrative: Write a story told entirely through a series of brief correspondences: telegrams or letters or emails between two characters. The correspondence should span several months or years, and reveal a gradually unfolding plot. Use distinct voices for each character, and include details that provide insight into their personalities and motivations. The story should build to an emotional climax, and the final letter should provide a satisfying resolution. The setting is a lighthouse keeper writing to his mother. He is working class and Scottish. He is struggling with the isolation of his posting. Write naturally and without cliches. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**The Lighthouse Keeper** 4 February 1959 Dear Mam, I am settled at Sgeir Bhan. The bothy is drier than it looked, and the lamp room has a fine brass rail. The stairs to the gallery are steep, but my legs are young. The wage is paid monthly, so I will send an order on Friday. Don’t spend it all on coal, though I know it is dear. The boatman says the weather will hold. I can see the mainland when the air is clear, which is a comfort. Your son, Ewan 8 February 1959 Dear Ewan, Got the order. I am not daft enough to spend it all on coal, but the single end is cold and I will not pretend otherwise. Mrs Docherty’s boy is at the docks now and she thinks he is grand because he wears a cap. You keep your socks dry and don’t let the salt stiffen your boots. Write when you can. Mam 19 March 1959 Dear Mam, The quiet here is not quiet. It is full of small noises: the lamp ticking as it cools, the chains in the store, gannets landing on the gallery like dropped plates. I have begun to talk to them. Only a wee word or two. There is no one else to answer. Ewan 23 March 1959 Dear Ewan, Talking to birds is no worse than talking to the women at the laundry. They talk all day and say nothing. But if you are lonely, son, write more. Paper is cheaper than a doctor. I have sent you a tin of shortbread. Don’t share it with the gannets or they will come back for more. Mam 11 June 1959 Dear Mam, The parcel came, though the tin was dented and one biscuit broken. I found something today in a drawer under the oilskins. A glass float, the size of a large apple, green as bottle water, with a bubble caught in the middle like a breath. Some keeper has bound it in fine copper wire and scratched a small lighthouse on the glass, and below it a woman’s name: Effie. When the lamp turns at night it throws a green star on the wall. I have put it on the sill. Ewan 15 June 1959 Dear Ewan, Effie will be long gone, likely. Leave the thing be, though it sounds bonny. Men keep bits of glass and call them company. Your father kept a herring knife with a broken handle and I told him it was no use. He said it had work in it yet. Don’t be like that. Come ashore when you can. Mam 2 October 1959 Dear Mam, I cannot come ashore yet. The relief man has a bad knee and the boat is delayed by swells. I am all right. The green star comes round the wall each night and I look for it. Do you remember the lights in the close at Christmas, when you put the candle in the window for Da? I think of that. Ewan 6 October 1959 Dear Ewan, I remember. I also remember you were too tired to wait for him and fell asleep in your boots. You were always one for waiting, even then. If the boat cannot come, keep your routine. Wind the clock, trim your nails, wash your face. The body needs small orders when the mind wants to run. Mam 21 January 1960 Mam, There was a storm three nights. I thought the tower would shake itself loose. I could not hear my own voice. I took the glass float down from the sill and held it in my coat pocket because I was feared it would break. When morning came I saw I had cut my hand on the wire. It is nothing. But I am tired, Mam. I have been tired since Da drowned. Ewan 25 January 1960 My son, Your hand wants cleaned, not pitied. I will say plain what I know: you went to that rock because you thought it would make you steady, and it has, but steady is not the same as buried. I have had a cough and the doctor says I must go into the infirmary for a few days. Nothing tragic. But if you can get leave, I would like you here. Not for me. For you. Mam 3 February 1960 Dear Mam, I have asked for relief. The superintendent at Oban says a man can take my place by the end of the month. I will come to Glasgow then. I wrapped Effie’s float in my spare shirt and put it in the sea chest. It is safe. I should have told you sooner about the tiredness. I thought if I stayed out here long enough I would earn the right to come back. Ewan 9 February 1960 Dear Ewan, You never had to earn a door. The month will pass. I am out of the infirmary and stronger than I was, though the nurse says I must not climb stairs too fast. I have your room aired. Bring the green glass if you like. I want to see what kept you company. And Ewan, when you come, knock once. I will know it is you. Mam 1 March 1960 Mam, You were sleeping when I came in, so I am writing this at the table instead of waking you. The train was late, but the close smelled the same: soap, coal smoke, and Mrs Docherty’s soup. I have put the green float on the window. The street lamp catches it and makes a wee star on your wall. I asked the superintendent for a shore post. He says there may be work at the signal station in Oban, not grand, but with people and a bus home. I am not running back to the rock. I am only coming back to myself. Your hand looked thin on the quilt, but your face is easier. I will make the tea when you wake. Your son, Ewan
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This epistolary story succeeds on nearly every level. The two voices are distinct and consistent: Ewan is restrained, observational, prone to understatement ("It is nothing"), while Mam is dry, practical, deflecting tenderness through housekeeping advice ("Paper is cheaper than a doctor"). The Scottish working-class idiom feels authentic rather than performed — "single end," "close," "feared," "bonny" — and neither character slips out of register across the year-long span. The plot unfolds gradually and organically: the glass float with "Effie" scratched on it is a lovely device, a relic of a previous keeper's loneliness that becomes Ewan's talisman, then a symbol of what he nearly becomes. The buried grief for the drowned father surfaces naturally in the storm letter, and the mother's response — "steady is not the same as buried" — is the emotional pivot, delivered with characteristic bluntness. The resolution (shore post at Oban, the final letter written at the table while she sleeps, the green star now on her wall) is satisfying without being saccharine; the closing image mirrors and completes the earlier one. Minor criticisms: the transformation is somewhat quick — Ewan moves from deep fatigue to "coming back to myself" within a few letters, though the seeds were planted early enough that it reads as earned. The mother's illness is a slightly conventional device for forcing the reunion. A couple of Mam's aphorisms ("The body needs small orders when the mind wants to run") verge on the writerly, a touch too polished for her. The final letter slightly over-explains the theme ("I am not running back to the rock. I am only coming back to myself") where the imagery alone might have carried it. Imagery is precise and fresh: gannets "landing like dropped plates," the float's bubble "like a breath," the lamp throwing "a green star on the wall." No purple prose, no clichés of note. The pacing across dated letters is tight; nothing meanders. + First-person unique perspective: Hacker Mindset — Score: 76.6
Prompt:
Hacker Mindset Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a reformed (now) white hat hacker who cannot help but notice exploitable weaknesses in both systems and people they encounter. They habitually look for vulnerabilities and exploit vectors. The narrative takes place during a first date at a restaurant, where they're trying to focus on human connection. It's going surprisingly well due to a discovered shared nerd-fandom (magic the gathering). Things go a little sideways when the date reveals a noticeably insecure phone unlock pattern, which protagonist can't help but comment on. They are then left to negotiate the fallout of this faux pas and attempt to salvage (or perhaps sabotage) the remainder of the date. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
Be present. That’s the assignment. First date. Nice restaurant. I can do normal. I repeat it like a mantra while my eyes snag on the host stand tablet running a build so old it probably thinks TLS 1.0 is futuristic. Don’t scan. Don’t assess. You’re not that person anymore. You’re here to laugh, ask questions, and maybe touch someone’s emotional life without leaving a footprint. The WiFi password is taped to the counter. Of course. Bright blue painter’s tape, black marker: Soup2Day!9. A laminated gift to every credential harvester within range. I feel the old itch, the one that used to be a full-body compulsion: enumerate devices, identify weak clients, imagine the phishing page that would make this place fold in ten minutes. I squash it. I’m white hat now. I write reports, not ransom notes. I help people patch. Mostly I try to patch the part of my brain that treats every room like a capture-the-flag. Then Elena comes back from the restroom, smiling, and I remember why I’m attempting this. She slides into the booth and says, “Okay, but if you’re playing a blue-control deck, I’m going to need you to explain why you enjoy suffering.” My chest does something unencrypted. We found the Magic thing twenty minutes ago, after I complimented the faded dragon on her phone case. Not just any dragon: a worn prerelease artifact, the kind that means someone has stuck with a hobby through expansions, breakups, and bad mana. I said Commander. She said obviously. The whole restaurant got quieter in the best way. Now we’re trading cards like war stories. She likes combo decks that look innocent until they aren’t. I like control, because control means watching, naming threats early, keeping chaos at a distance. That tells her too much about me, probably. I used to believe control was safety. Now I know it’s just a prettier word for fear. But she laughs at my joke about counterspells being emotional boundaries, and I think: maybe this is a vulnerability you don’t need to patch. Her phone lights up. Notification. She lifts it to dismiss it, and my vision narrows. Unlock pattern. Nine dots. Four points. Starts top left, drops to bottom left, zips right, flicks up. An L with a little tail. Predictable. Short. Probably repeated daily until the screen is a greasy map of exactly where her finger goes. I can see the smudge trail even in candlelight. It’s not that I’m trying to invade her privacy. It’s that my brain has already filed the observation before I can revoke access. Don’t say anything. You are not the security team. You are a person on a date. Ask about her sideboard. Ask whether she’s ever been to a Grand Prix. Ask anything except— “That’s a really weak unlock pattern.” The words leave me with cheerful precision, like a packet that knows exactly where it’s going. Her smile doesn’t vanish. It compiles an error. I want to swallow the sentence back, but my mouth is still running legacy code. I tell her it’s short, four points, and the smudges basically draw it for anyone. I say I’m sorry. I say I notice stuff. Elena sets the phone face down. In my head it’s a port closing. She repeats that I noticed her unlock pattern. On a date. I know. She asks if I’m one of those people who can guess a password from a birthday and a dog’s name. There’s a test under it. I know it. I tell her no: I used to be worse. I’m trying to be better. Better. Such a vague version. Better than the years when I saw humans as attack surfaces, when empathy was just another input to model. Better than the time I convinced myself that exposing a flaw was kindness. Better than the fact that I’m trying to build trust and my first instinct was to point out the crack in her armor. She stirs her drink and asks what else I’ve noticed. Oh no. This is the part where I can either be honest or be employable. I list them before I can edit: the WiFi password taped to the counter, the outdated host tablet, the card reader sticker with a serial number that probably shouldn’t be public, the way she keeps her wallet in a left jacket pocket that’s easy for someone passing behind her to reach. Her eyebrows rise. I add, foolishly, that she rotates her ring when she’s nervous. The ring stops rotating. I brace. This is where people usually decide I’m creepy. The math is unfair: observation isn’t intent, noticing a weakness doesn’t mean I want to exploit it, and for me vigilance used to be survival. But explaining turns intimacy into a deposition. So I wait. Elena looks at me for a long moment, then asks what she should do. The question is a trap. If I lecture, I become a manual. If I deflect, I seem evasive. If I gloat, date over. I choose humility with a patch note. I tell her to change the pattern, make it longer, avoid obvious shapes, maybe use a passcode or biometrics if she trusts them. Don’t let the screen get so smudgy it confesses. Maybe mention the WiFi sign helps the wrong people. She nods slowly and says I could’ve just said that without making her feel like her phone was naked. Yeah. I let myself feel the burn. I tell her that was my mistake: I pointed out a vulnerability when she didn’t ask for a security review. It was rude. I’m sorry. She smiles, just slightly. Maybe this is where I sabotage us by explaining threat models. Maybe this is where I salvage us by shutting up. I look at the WiFi password, her phone, the dragon on her case. Magic taught me control isn’t answering every threat; it’s protecting the win condition. Mine is simple: be curious, be kind, be present. “Tell me about your deck,” I say.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece executes the prompt well: first-person internal monologue dominates, the white-hat hacker's compulsive vulnerability-scanning is established immediately (host tablet, taped WiFi password), the MTG connection is woven in naturally and thematically (control decks as a metaphor for the protagonist's fear), and the unlock-pattern faux pas lands at the right moment with genuine cringe. The voice is consistent—tech metaphors ("compiles an error," "port closing," "patch note") are used as the character's cognitive filter rather than decoration, which is the right choice. The fallout negotiation is handled with some nuance: Elena neither storms off nor forgives instantly; she tests, pushes back ("you could've just said that without making her feel like her phone was naked"), and the protagonist's self-awareness ("observation isn't intent... but explaining turns intimacy into a deposition") feels earned by the character's history. The ending ties back to the win-condition metaphor without being saccharine. Weaknesses: the tech-metaphor density occasionally tips into cleverness-over-feeling ("my chest does something unencrypted" is a bit precious). Elena is somewhat underdrawn—she exists mostly as a test-giver and reactor, and her forgiveness arrives a touch quickly given how alarming the protagonist's confession (wallet pocket, nervous ring-rotation) actually is; a real person might reasonably be more rattled. The "reformed hacker" backstory is asserted rather than shown in any concrete incident, so the transformation is more stated than dramatized. Some beats (the "be present" mantra, the closing "be curious, be kind, be present") flirt with the formulaic. Still, the prose flows well, the humor lands, the pacing is tight, and the emotional complexity—shame, compulsion, longing to connect—is genuinely present rather than gestured at. + First-person unique perspective: Overthinking It — Score: 58.7
Prompt:
Overthinking It Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of an intelligent 8th-grade girl with social anxiety who has developed a crush on a classmate. The narrative takes place during a group science project where they're paired together, as she cycles through rehearsed conversations while second-guessing each potential approach. Her inner thoughts should reveal the gap between her articulate internal voice and her difficulty expressing herself aloud, her fears of coming across as desperate or weird, and the exhausting process of monitoring her every word, expression, and movement for potential embarrassment. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
Mr. Alvarez says partners and my brain rearranges the universe into one terrifying sentence: You are with Eli Chen. For three weeks. On the genetics project. I keep my eyes on the whiteboard, because if I look at him I will stop breathing or smile like a grimace. There are twenty-six students in eighth-grade science, and random seating charts have placed me beside the one person I cannot afford to like. Like is a soft word. Like is what you call a song. What I feel for Eli is more like a system error, a warning sounding in my skull every time he borrows a pencil: alert, alert, you are too aware of his hands. Okay. Manageable. It is only science. It is only Eli. I can be normal. I can say, Hey, want to divide the research sections? and sound like someone who has never rehearsed a conversation with her ceiling fan. I could say, We should make an outline first, because that is what responsible group members say. Concise. Cooperative. Not desperate. It does not say I noticed you changed your handwriting after art class. It does not say I kept a gum wrapper you dropped because it was stupid and somehow important. No. It says: I am easy to work with. I have boundaries. I am not weird. Except. If I say outline first, will that make me sound bossy? Maybe he hates bossy girls. Maybe he thinks organized people are annoying. Maybe he wants to joke around, and I’ll become the person who corrects him. He’ll look at me with polite disappointment, the expression I imagine teachers using before they say, Let’s try that again. Or worse: he’ll laugh. Not cruelly. Just a soft, surprised laugh, like he didn’t expect me to talk. I am the girl who answers only when called on, whose voice sometimes arrives half a second too late, smaller than the thought behind it. My inside voice is fluent. My inside voice could explain genetics with perfect pacing. My outside voice acts like it has forgotten how to use doors. I glance at Eli. Mistake. He is opening his notebook, and the blue cover has a sticker of a raccoon eating pizza. Of course he has a ridiculous sticker. Of course it makes me want to ask about it, which would be casual if I could ask without sounding like I’m interrogating his school supplies. Cool sticker. Simple. Safe. He would say, Thanks, my cousin gave it to me, and we would be two regular people discussing a regular object. But what if my tone comes out too high? What if I say cool like I’m performing? What if I say sticker like it personally offended me? Then the smell hits: ammonia, sharp and chemical, curling up from the floor near the lab stations. The custodian must have mopped during lunch, or someone spilled cleaner by the sink. It clings to the air and stings the back of my nose, and for a second my mental script dissolves into white static. Ammonia. Why does it smell like a hospital? Like a cartoon of broken glass? Like my brain being scrubbed? I inhale too fast and my eyes water. Perfect. Nothing says confident partner like crying before the rubric is handed out. The scent drags through my next thought: Was I supposed to ask about Punnett squares? Do peas have alleles? Does ammonia have alleles? Everything is suddenly triangles and stinging. Eli shifts in his chair. I immediately adjust my posture. Shoulders neutral. Not too stiff. Not slouched like I’m trying to dissolve into the lab table. Hands flat on the notebook—too intense. Hands in lap—too secretive. One hand on the table, one on the pen. Great. Now I look prepared to take notes on my own panic. My face is doing something. I attempt pleasant, which probably looks like a wavy line drawn by an earthquake. I relax my eyebrows. I unclench my jaw. I remember blinking is necessary and then blink five times in a row, as if my eyelids are applauding my incompetence. I try composing the sentence in advance. If I say hi, should I add his name? Hi, Eli. Too formal, like I’m calling him to a dentist appointment. Hey. Too abrupt. Hey, Eli. Too friendly? Hello. Absolutely no; hello belongs to customer service and grandmothers. I test the phrase silently, moving my tongue against my teeth. The word changes each time, losing meaning, becoming just sound, a shape my mouth has to make while my brain watches from behind glass. If I speak too quickly, I’ll trip. If I speak too slowly, he’ll wait, and waiting turns seconds into spotlights. Every possible version of me is being filmed, reviewed, archived, and punished for content I haven’t even produced yet. And if I laugh too loudly? If I touch my hair? If my elbow bumps his and I die? I catalog each disaster before it occurs. It is exhausting, being both performer and audience, critic and stage manager of my own embarrassment. Okay. New plan. Let him speak first. That is safe. Passive. The social equivalent of hiding behind a bush during a nature documentary. If he says, Where should we start? I can answer, Maybe research first? with a question mark so it doesn’t sound demanding. If he says nothing, I will simply sit here until old age takes me. But my heart is beating under my ribs like a fire alarm, and what if he hears it? What if he thinks I’m stuck-up? Weird? Mad? If he asks why I’m quiet, what am I supposed to say? The truth is too large: your elbow is two inches from mine, and my entire personality has become a smoke detector. Still. I open my mouth. Just once. Just for the sentence. Say hi. Say project. Say anything ordinary. My voice trembles at the edge of me, tiny and bright, waiting for permission it knows I may not give.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a strong execution of the prompt: an 8th-grade girl with social anxiety, internal monologue dominant, crush on lab partner Eli, rehearsing and second-guessing. The voice is articulate and self-aware, matching the brief's requirement of a gap between fluent inner voice and faltering outer voice ("My inside voice is fluent... My outside voice acts like it has forgotten how to use doors" — an excellent line). The cycling through greeting options (Hi/Hey/Hello) is authentic to anxious cognition, and the posture-monitoring passage ("Hands flat on the notebook—too intense...") captures the exhausting self-surveillance requested. Strengths: consistent first-person voice, age-appropriate but intelligent diction, humor that arises naturally from anxiety ("eyelids are applauding my incompetence"), concrete grounding in the science classroom (Punnett squares, genetics project, raccoon sticker). The ending withholds resolution appropriately — she's at the edge of speaking, no unearned breakthrough. Weaknesses: The ammonia smell passage is an odd intrusion — it reads like an injected sensory disruption that doesn't quite earn its prominence and briefly muddles the focus ("Does ammonia have alleles?" is charming but the sequence feels like padding toward word count). Some metaphors stack too densely (smoke detector, fire alarm, performer/audience/critic/stage manager in quick succession), tipping toward overwrought in places. The piece is essentially one sustained beat — no arc or development beyond mounting anxiety — which is faithful to the prompt but limits emotional range; the anxiety is well-rendered but somewhat one-note, with little nuance beyond fear. A few similes strain ("a wavy line drawn by an earthquake"). No dialogue is spoken aloud, so dialogue criteria are largely inapplicable, though the imagined exchanges are handled well. The prose occasionally performs cleverness rather than letting the character simply think. Overall: a skilled, engaging, mostly disciplined piece that fulfills the prompt with genuine voice, slightly over-decorated and structurally static. + First-person unique perspective: Rehearsing Rejection — Score: 81.2
Prompt:
Rehearsing Rejection Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of someone with borderline personality disorder who frequently plays out worst-case scenarios of how friends and loved ones might judge them. They construct elaborate internal dialogues, complete with imagined criticisms and their own defensive responses. The narrative takes place as they prepare to meet a close friend & recent lover, who has been somewhat distant lately, triggering their abandonment fears. Their inner monologue should reveal how they cycle between anticipating rejection, mentally rehearsing confrontations, and developing preemptive resentments as protective measures. Incorporate the *actual* events & interactions that are *not* in fact judgemental or involving rejection (in fact, the opposite), and represent how these are interpreted, how the validation & love is desperately felt & needed -- and then immediately questioned. Capture the cognitive dissonance in this struggle. Include moments where they briefly recognize the pattern but struggle to interrupt it, showing limited (and selective) self awareness, competing with the compelling nature of these imagined scenarios. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
In the hallway mirror, I catch myself leaning forward as if the glass might tell me what Jules hasn’t texted. Shoulders up. Jaw tight. Hands in my pockets, then out, then smoothing my shirt like I can iron the panic out of my body. I look like someone waiting to be sentenced. I turn away before I can practice a face that says I don’t care. Jules’s message is still on the screen: *Running a little late, sorry. Order me something? Can’t wait to see you.* A little late. Not *so sorry*, not *I feel terrible*. Just *a little*, as if the waiting isn’t already a message. As if the distance has already started and this is only the polite opening act. *Can’t wait to see you* could mean anything. People say that when they’re trying to convince themselves. People say that right before they say something else. I rehearse it while I put my phone face-down, then flip it over again. He’ll come in looking careful. That soft, cautious face people make when they’ve already decided but want to be kind about it. He’ll sit too close or too far away and say, *Hey, thanks for waiting*, and I’ll say, *You’re late*, too sharp, because I can’t help it. Then he’ll say, *I know, I’m sorry, things have been complicated*, and I’ll think, *Just say it. Stop wrapping it in weather.* In my head, he says, *I think we’re moving too fast.* In my head, I say, *I never asked you to move at all.* That’s the part I practice most: the clean exit. The line that makes me sound untouched. If he says, *This isn’t working*, I’ll say, *I was thinking the same thing.* If he says, *You’re too intense*, I’ll say, *You were never deep enough to handle it.* If he says, *I care about you, but—* I’ll laugh. Not cruelly. Just enough to show I’m not destroyed. Just enough to make him regret the sentence he hasn’t finished. He hasn’t even arrived and I have already built the courtroom. I have already assigned him his role: the reasonable one, the exhausted one, the person who tried but can’t keep doing this. I have already written my defense. I have already become the version of myself who doesn’t need him, which is the only version I can trust to survive. And then the door opens. Jules comes in with rain on his jacket and a paper bag in one hand. He looks around, finds me, and his whole face changes. Not careful. Not cautious. Open. *There you are,* he says, slightly out of breath. *I brought you that lemon thing you like. The bakery was closing and I ran like an idiot.* For one second, the relief is so physical it nearly buckles me. He remembered. He ran. He is here with rain on his shoulders and my favorite pastry in a bag, smiling like he means it. For one second, I let myself be loved by it. Then the next second arrives. *Why didn’t you text that you were stopping there?* I think. *Why make me wait without knowing? Why give me something sweet after making me afraid? Is this compensation? Is this the softening before the blow?* He sits beside me, close enough that our knees almost touch, and says, *I missed you this week.* My chest does something stupid and hopeful. I want to press the words into my skin. I want to eat them before they can be taken back. *I missed you too*, I say, but inside I’m already inspecting the sentence. Missed me how? Missed me like you miss a habit? Like you miss someone you feel guilty about? Like you miss a person you’re preparing to lose? He pulls out his phone and glances at it, then frowns. There it is. *You’re distracted*, I think. *You’re here but not here. You’re already elsewhere, already with whoever or whatever matters more. You brought me a lemon thing so I won’t notice the exit forming.* In my head, I say, *If you need to go, just go.* In my head, he says, *You always assume the worst.* In my head, I say, *You always give me reasons to.* But out loud, he says, *Sorry. Work’s been insane. I keep thinking they’ll call me back in ten minutes.* He puts the phone face-down on the table. *I don’t want to be distracted with you.* The tenderness hits me sideways. I want to cry. I want to accuse him. Both impulses arrive together, tangled, indistinguishable. *I don’t want to be distracted with you* is exactly what I needed to hear, and because I needed it, I immediately suspect it. People say what you want to hear when they’re trying to avoid the thing they mean. Or they mean it in the moment and then stop meaning it later. Which is worse? Maybe both. Maybe neither. Maybe I am so hungry for reassurance that I can’t digest it when it comes. He pushes the bag toward me. *Eat it before it gets sad.* I take a bite. It’s sweet and sharp and ridiculous. He watches me with a little grin, and for a moment I feel real. I feel chosen. I feel like someone who can be met at a café on a rainy evening without having to armor every inch of herself first. Then my mind whispers, *He’s being nice because he feels guilty.* I hate it. I hate how quickly the gift becomes evidence. I hate that love has to pass through my suspicion before I’m allowed to feel it. I hate that I am simultaneously desperate for him to say *I’m not leaving* and convinced that if he says it, he’s lying. *Can we talk later?* he asks. *There’s something I want to tell you.* My body goes cold. This is it. The rehearsed scene. The careful voice. The speech about boundaries and timing and how I’m too much in ways he can explain gently but not survive. I hear myself say, *Okay.* Inside, I am already packing. Inside, I am saying, *Fine, I knew it. I always knew. You don’t get to act wounded when you’re the one leaving.* Inside, I am resenting him for making me listen, for making me sit still, for making me hope only to take it away. Inside, I am punishing him in advance. He takes a breath. *My mom’s in the hospital. It happened last week and I didn’t know how to say it. I’ve been distant because every time I tried, I shut down. I’m sorry. I don’t want you to think this is about you.* The words land slowly, like snow on warm pavement. Not rejection. Not abandonment. Fear. Grief. A reason that has nothing to do with my worth and everything to do with his life. I feel the scaffolding inside me wobble. I had built the whole tragedy already. I had memorized my lines. I had even forgiven him for leaving in the cruel, triumphant way you forgive someone only after you’ve decided they’ve wronged you. And now he’s here, asking me to be closer instead of preparing me to be gone. *I should have told you sooner,* he says. *I was scared. I didn’t want to burden you.* The old script flares up instantly: *Burden? You think I can’t handle it? You think love is something you ration when things get hard?* I want to be angry. Anger feels safer than the ache opening under it. If I’m angry, I don’t have to admit how badly I wanted him to need me. If I’m angry, I don’t have to risk believing he does. But I look at his hands, wrapped around his coffee, and his eyes, tired and earnest, and something in me recognizes the pattern. Not all of it. Not enough to stop it. Just enough to see it moving. *This is the part where I turn care into betrayal*, I think. *This is the part where I rehearse rejection before it happens so it can’t surprise me. This is the part where I protect myself from loss by losing you first.* I know it. I know it and I still feel the pull of it, magnetic and familiar, like a road I’ve driven so many times my hands remember the turns. *I’m glad you told me,* I say, and my voice is smaller than I want it to be. He reaches across the table and covers my hand with his. His palm is warm. I want to pull away. I want to hold on. I do both for a second, my fingers tense under his, then slowly, deliberately, I turn my hand over and let him take it. *Can I ask you something?* he says. *Yeah.* *When I’m quiet, can you tell me what you’re afraid of instead of fighting me for it?* The question is gentle, but it feels like a blade because it’s fair. Because it’s not an accusation. Because it asks me to do the thing I most want and most dread: say the need without turning it into a weapon. *I’ll try,* I say. He nods, and his thumb brushes once over my knuckles. *I’m not trying to leave you,* he says. *I’m trying to figure out how to stay.* I believe him. I don’t. I believe him. I don’t. Both sentences sit in me at the same time, bright and heavy, and I don’t know which one will win. I want to ask him to say it again. I want to tell him not to bother because repetition won’t fix this. I want to be soothed and I want to be proven right and I want, more than either, to stop needing proof so badly. He squeezes my hand. *Hey,* he says. *I’m here.* I look at him, and for a moment I let the words be just words. Not a test. Not a prelude. Not a kindness arranged around an absence. Just him, saying what he means, while I try to learn how to receive it without immediately rehearsing its loss. Outside, the rain picks up. Inside, my heart is still armored, still scanning, still half-turned toward the door. But I don’t get up. I don’t make the clean exit. I stay seated with my hand in his, tasting lemon and fear and something fragile that might, if I don’t crush it, be trust.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is an accomplished piece of internal monologue that fulfills nearly every requirement of the prompt with precision and craft. The narrator's BPD-coded cognition—preemptive resentment, rehearsed confrontations, imagined dialogues with assigned lines for the other person—is rendered convincingly and with psychological specificity. The structure is smart: the imagined rejection scenarios are vivid enough to feel real, then the actual events (the lemon pastry, the lateness explained by work, the "something to tell you" that turns out to be a hospitalized mother) systematically contradict the narrator's projections, exactly as instructed. The moment where the narrator recognizes the pattern ("This is the part where I turn care into betrayal") but can't fully interrupt it captures the requested limited, selective self-awareness. The closing "I believe him. I don't." captures cognitive dissonance without resolving it falsely. Strengths: the prose is controlled and rhythmic, with short declarative sentences that mirror hypervigilance; imagery ("built the courtroom," "snow on warm pavement," "eat it before it gets sad") is fresh without being ornamental; the emotional register is complex—relief, suspicion, anger, hunger for reassurance all tangled together; the ending resists both false redemption and melodrama. Weaknesses: some of the interpretive moves are slightly repetitive (the "then the next second arrives" pivot is used several times); the mother-in-hospital reveal is a familiar device for "the distance wasn't about you"; occasionally the narrator's self-analysis is a touch too articulate, edging toward telling ("I hate that love has to pass through my suspicion"); Jules's dialogue ("I'm trying to figure out how to stay") is a bit polished for a tired, grieving man. The ending's fragile hope is earned rather than imposed, though it flirts with a slightly neat resolution. These are minor quibbles against a genuinely strong piece. + Physical-spatial: Blood Debt — Score: 75.9
Prompt:
"Blood Debt" Write a vivid third-person narrative depicting an unsanctioned underground duel between two talented but hot-headed martial artists. Their schools have been embroiled in a generations-old rivalry, and despite strict prohibitions from their masters, these two younger fighters arrange a secret confrontation fueled by personal pride and simmering animosity. - **One fighter** represents **Jigen-ryū**, a traditional, aggressive style practiced historically by elite samurai clans. Its practitioners emphasize explosive offense, decisive strikes, and overwhelming speed. Known historically for their arrogance and disdain toward outsiders, practitioners consider their art superior and untouchable. - **The opposing fighter** employs a form of historical **Piguaquan**, a Chinese martial art traditionally practiced by commoners, bodyguards, and street fighters. This style emphasizes whipping, circular strikes, rapid footwork, unpredictable angles of attack, and evasive maneuvers. Practitioners often come from lower social classes and view the traditional elite as pretentious and detached from true combat effectiveness. The fight takes place in the crumbling ruins of an abandoned temple, now functioning as a hidden arena for illicit duels. Passionate supporters from both factions surround them, wagering money, pride, and reputation on the outcome. **Essential Instructions:** Maintain absolute physical coherence throughout—clearly track fighters' positions relative to each other and their environment. Precisely depict strikes, counters, momentum shifts, and spatial dynamics, allowing readers to clearly visualize the mechanics and choreography of the fight at every moment. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Blood Debt** The abandoned temple had no name left, only a hollow hall where the roof had fallen in and moss stitched cracked flagstones. Lanterns hung from crooked poles at the four corners of the fighting circle. To the north stood the ruined altar; to the south, broken doors with lookouts in shadow. Around them, gamblers, students, and thieves pressed close against an eighteen-pace ring of packed earth. Jirō entered from the north, shoulders squared, chin lifted. He wore a red-and-black armband tied above his left elbow. Across the circle, Mei came from the south, scowling, her red-and-black band wound around her right forearm. Jigen-ryū disciples behind him slapped the floor, crying for one decisive blow. Piguaquan supporters behind her laughed, wagering copper, calling the samurai school a peacock that had forgotten how to bleed. The duel had been forbidden by both masters, yet arranged anyway: a shove in a market lane, a broken training badge, words too hot to swallow. Jirō had called Mei’s art gutter dancing. Mei had called his a corpse polished with gold. An old man dropped a coin. Jirō moved before it landed. From the north edge he shot south in two sliding steps, right foot planting, right hand rising and falling like a hatchet. Mei stood six paces away, facing him. Instead of meeting the strike, she stepped to her right, toward the east, angling outside his arm. Jirō’s hammerfist split empty air. His momentum carried him half a pace too far. Mei’s right arm snapped sideways in a whipping arc, knuckles raking his left ribs. The crowd roared. Jirō did not retreat. He pivoted on his left foot, turning east toward her, and drove a rising forearm at her jaw. Mei leaned back, the bone missing her chin, and circled farther east. Jirō followed with straight advances: step, strike; step, strike. Each attack came down the shortest line, forcing Mei backward along the eastern side of the ring. His knuckle strike caught her shoulder. Her counter slipped off his raised elbow. Behind Mei, the broken stump of an eastern pillar rose waist-high. Jirō surged forward, certain he had trapped her. As his lead foot came down, she planted her left hand on the pillar’s edge and swung her body north around the stone. Jirō’s charge followed a heartbeat too late. His shoulder struck the pillar instead of her back. He jarred, but was already turning, left foot dragging across the earth. Mei used the pillar as a pivot. Her right arm looped over his descending guard, pulling his wrist down and across while her left palm cracked against the side of his neck. Jirō staggered northeast toward the altar. Mei pursued in a curved path, strikes coming from odd angles: backhand, low palm, an elbow flicking off his collarbone as he tried to square his hips. The Jigen-ryū supporters screamed warnings. The Pigua crowd beat the floor. Someone shouted Jirō’s name; another answered with Mei’s. At the altar’s edge, Jirō’s heel struck broken stone. He stopped retreating. When Mei whipped another right-hand strike toward his temple, he ducked into it, letting the blow graze his ear, and rammed his shoulder into her midsection. The impact drove her south, back toward center. Jirō followed, face slick with blood. He threw a short right fist to her sternum. Mei twisted, taking the strike on her shoulder, and answered with a circular forearm smash to his biceps. Pain numbed his arm, but he caught her wrist. Only an instant. Mei’s free hand chopped down on his elbow. He released her. She spun counterclockwise, putting her body between his trapped arm and the open floor, and swept her low foot across his ankle. Jirō hopped back, nearly falling, and the fight reset near the center: Jirō north, Mei south, both breathing hard, both bleeding. The lookouts by the southern doors shifted. Neither fighter saw the old man raise his hand. Jirō wiped his mouth with his red-and-black band. Mei lowered her stance, fingers loose. Around them the lanterns smoked. The crowd leaned inward like a tide about to break. Then Jirō launched south for the final time. He came with everything his school prized: one explosive step, one committed strike. His right fist descended toward Mei’s collarbone while his left hand guarded high. Mei feinted to her right, toward the east, the same angle she had used at the opening. Jirō’s eyes flicked that way, and his hips began to turn to cut her off. But Mei did not go east. She dropped her weight and cut to her left, west, slipping under his falling arm on the inside of his right side. Jirō realized the deception too late. His strike hit only air. His body followed the blow, carried south by its own force. Mei pivoted on her right foot, facing his exposed flank. Her left arm whipped across the back of his knee. Her right elbow snapped upward into his jaw. Jirō’s head jerked back. His unsupported leg buckled. He crashed to one knee, one hand slapping the ground. For a breath, the hall went silent except for lantern flames. Mei stood a pace southwest of him, chest heaving, blood dripping from her split knuckles. She did not kick him while he was down. The position itself was verdict: she upright, he kneeling; she inside his guard, he outside hers. Jirō tried to rise. His leg trembled, then refused. A Jigen-ryū senior lunged into the ring to help him, and Piguaquan bodies surged forward to block the way. Shouts became shoves. The old man rang a cracked bell three times. Mei backed toward the southern doors, supporters closing around her. Across the chaos, Jirō remained on one knee by the center of the ruined hall, staring at the place where she had stood. His armband was torn, his face pale with fury and shame. The debt had been paid in blood, but no one looked settled. The rivalry, older than either fighter, took another mark and waited for the next forbidden circle.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a disciplined, well-crafted fight narrative. Its greatest strength is spatial coherence: the piece anchors the arena with cardinal directions (altar north, doors south, pillar east), tracks both fighters' positions through every exchange, and uses the environment (the pillar, the altar edge) as active choreography rather than decoration. The choreography is legible—each strike, pivot, and momentum shift can be visualized, and the final feint-east/cut-west deception is a satisfying tactical payoff that mirrors the opening exchange. The styles are well differentiated: Jigen-ryū as linear, committed, explosive offense; Piguaquan as circular, evasive, angle-hunting. The prose is lean and controlled, mostly showing rather than telling, with a few effective images ("a corpse polished with gold," "the crowd leaned inward like a tide about to break"). Weaknesses: the characters are thin. Jirō and Mei are defined almost entirely by their schools; their personal animus is summarized in two lines of backstory rather than dramatized, so the "personal pride and simmering animosity" feels generic. The crowd is a monolith. The ending is competent but somewhat formulaic—the "rivalry continues" coda is the expected beat, and the ominous old man raising his hand hints at a larger plot that never pays off, feeling like an unfinished thread. Some minor incoherence: the armbands are both "red-and-black," which muddles the factional color-coding the piece seems to set up. Dialogue is nearly absent (appropriate for the piece, but the trash-talk insults are efficient if slight). Emotionally, the piece engages through kinetic tension rather than depth; it is exciting but not especially moving. A few phrases ("The position itself was verdict") flirt with over-compression but mostly land. Overall: a strong, coherent, professional piece of fight writing that lacks the character depth and thematic resonance of a masterpiece. Prompt:
**"Breaking Formation"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a street dancer from a rough neighborhood who's won a scholarship to an elite K-pop training academy in Seoul. Desperately out of place culturally and technically, they struggle with a militaristically precise choreography that contradicts everything about their improvisational background. The punishing rehearsal takes place under a famous instructor known for breaking students to remake them, who sees potential in the narrator's raw talent but not their attitude. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—each dance move, position shift, and spatial relationship must be tracked with precision throughout the studio. Paint an exceptionally vivid kinetic picture through descriptions that capture not just movement but the contrast between the narrator's fluid, expressive style and the mechanical precision demanded. Their internal monologue should reveal culture shock, class anxiety, and the threatening realization that success here might mean losing their authentic movement voice. Include technical terminology that highlights the collision of street and commercial styles, moments when muscle memory betrays them, and a crucial decision point about whether to conform or rebel. Physical clarity is essential—readers must be able to visualize exactly how bodies move through space, how rhythms align or clash, and how the protagonist's body struggles against unfamiliar discipline. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The speakers in each corner of Studio A blast the same track, synchronized to the millisecond and just a hair too loud. The bass presses against my sternum before the count lands, as if the room is trying to start my heart for me. Mirror north wall. Door south. Five tape marks in a straight line. I am on the center mark, Minji one arm’s length to my left, Soo-ah one arm’s length to my right. Behind us, Instructor Noh paces the empty strip between our reflections and the door. Everyone calls her “Teacher Noh,” but in the hallway they say she broke three debut groups before they debuted. She says, “From the top. Shoulders square. No extra breath.” My sneakers are too bright against the pale floor. The other trainees wear identical black practice shoes, socks folded, hair pinned. I wear what my cousin sent from home: neon green, scuffed at the toe, lucky. Lucky is a stupid word here. My mother’s eviction notice is folded in my bag, sharp as a blade. The track starts. One, two, three, four— Count one: right foot slides east into second position, wider than hips. Arms snap into a high V, elbows locked, wrists knife-straight, palms facing the mirror. My body wants to swing into the beat, to let the V become a groove, a lazy opening like a cypher response. Instead I must make geometry. Count two: left foot closes. Arms cut down to a horizontal T. Chin drops exactly two inches. Minji’s fingertips almost brush mine. I feel the line as a threat: if I am one centimeter late, I dirty all of us. Count three: right shoulder isolation. Only the shoulder lifts. Hip stays square. Neck stays long. In my old basement jams, a shoulder hit would come with chest, with face, with a growl in the ribs. Here, the rib cage is a locked box. Count four: left shoulder isolation. Head snaps to the mirror. My reflection looks like someone wearing my skin too tightly. Counts five and six: plié, chest caves, arms wrap around ribs; rise onto balls of feet, arms unfold straight north, palms out. This is the part the company calls “the idol reveal.” I call it a prison door opening. My quads shake. The music is loud enough to rattle the water bottle by the south wall. Count seven: right hand salutes beside temple, fingers flat; left arm pins to my side. Count eight: hold. Eyes forward. Breath invisible. Teacher Noh stops the music. The sudden silence rings in all four corners. “Ji-woo,” she says. My Korean name, the one on the scholarship file, not the name my mother calls. “Again. Alone.” The others step back to the wall, east and west, leaving me on the center mark. I can see their faces in the mirror: curious, relieved, hungry. I am the charity case, the foreigner, the street kid with a raw style that looked good on camera until it touched their system. She restarts the track. The speakers punch the beat into my spine. Count one. I open right, arms high. My hips try to follow with a bounce, a pocket from the block parties where we danced on cracked asphalt and the bass came from a car trunk. I clamp it down. Count two. Close. Arms T. But my left heel drifts off the tape. Teacher Noh’s baton taps her palm. “Your foot is a soldier,” she says. “Not a tourist.” Count three. Right shoulder. I hit it too hard, chest popping with it. A street accent. A krump scar. Her eyes narrow. “Again.” We do it again. And again. On the fourth run, she walks behind me and presses two fingers between my shoulder blades, forcing them down. “You dance like you are arguing with the floor,” she says. “The floor is not your enemy. It is your stage.” I almost laugh. The floor has always been my enemy and my mother. Concrete, gym tile, cardboard, train platform. You learn to talk to it before you learn to ignore it. On the fifth run, she stands in front of me, close enough that I can smell mint tea and cold metal. “You have power,” she says, quiet, in English, maybe to make sure I understand. “But power without shape is noise. I will not let you be noise.” Then, louder: “Full formation. Final phrase. If center is dirty, everyone runs stairs.” Minji and Soo-ah return to my left and right. Yuna and Hae-in fill the outer marks. Five bodies, one line. The mirror multiplies us into an army. The count starts. One: right foot east, high V. I feel the exact distance between my wrist and Soo-ah’s. Two: close, T, chin. Three: right shoulder. Four: left shoulder. Five: plié, chest in. Six: rise, arms forward. Seven: salute. Eight— At eight, the choreography says freeze. Eyes in the mirror. Nothing moves. But the music has a ghost note, a tiny snare flick between eight and the next one. My body knows it before my brain approves. In the basement, we would ride that flick. A wave from hip to sternum to fingertip. A secret sentence inside the stop. Teacher Noh is watching my reflection. I have one second. If I freeze, I become clean. If I move, I become myself. Success here may require the first. Survival may require the second. I choose the smaller rebellion. I hold the salute, but inside the hold I let the wave start at my right hip, roll through my ribs, travel up my locked right arm, and end in the tips of my fingers without changing the angle. It is not a break. It is not a bounce. It is a ripple under ice. The line stays perfect. The count stays perfect. My voice slips through anyway. In the mirror, Teacher Noh’s face does not change. But her baton stops tapping. “Again,” she says. The speakers inhale. The bass hits. My right foot slides east.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a tightly controlled, well-executed piece. The spatial coherence demanded by the prompt is delivered with unusual discipline: the studio is mapped (mirror north, door south, tape marks, positions of Minji and Soo-ah at arm's length), and every count of the choreography is tracked move by move, so the reader can genuinely visualize the formation. The count-by-count structure is a smart formal choice—it enacts the militaristic precision the narrator is fighting against. The central conflict is handled with nuance. The narrator's street vocabulary ("cypher response," "krump scar," "pocket from the block parties") collides convincingly with the academy's language of soldiers, geometry, and cleanliness. The "smaller rebellion" resolution—the wave inside the frozen salute—is the piece's best idea: it dramatizes the conform/rebel decision without a cheap victory, and Teacher Noh's non-reaction (the baton stops tapping) is a well-earned, understated beat. Weaknesses: the prose occasionally strains for effect ("The floor has always been my enemy and my mother" is a striking but slightly confusing metaphor; "prison door opening" is a bit on-the-nose). The eviction notice and "charity case" beats are efficient but somewhat familiar class-anxiety shorthand. Some lines ("Lucky is a stupid word here") flirt with preciosity. The dialogue is sparse and functional—Noh's aphorisms ("Your foot is a soldier. Not a tourist") are effective but slightly writerly. The ending loops back to the opening count, which is elegant, though the overall arc is modest: a single scene, well-rendered, without much narrative risk taken beyond the final choice. Still, the piece shows rather than tells, maintains voice, and earns its quiet ambiguity.
